questions.question: Harry Hess's 1962 seafloor-spreading proposal said mid-ocean ridges produce new crust that pushes older crust outward like a conveyor belt. What direct evidence in the early 1960s sealed the case for plate tectonics?
questions.answer: Symmetric magnetic-stripe patterns mirrored on both sides of mid-ocean ridges, recording magnetic-field reversals as new crust formed
choices: Symmetric magnetic-stripe patterns mirrored on both sides of mid-ocean ridges, recording magnetic-field reversals as new crust formed
Direct sonar imaging of underground rivers flowing beneath the Atlantic that pushed the continents apart slowly
Photographs from early Sputnik satellites showing the continents visibly moving from orbit each year
A Soviet drilling expedition that found a single continuous fossil layer connecting Europe and Africa
questions.context: Vine, Matthews, and Morley (1963) showed the pattern: as new ocean crust cools at the ridge, iron-rich minerals lock in Earth's current magnetic-field direction. Earth flips its field every few hundred thousand years on average, so the ocean floor reads like a tape recording — and the stripes are mirror-symmetric on either side of the ridge, exactly as Wegener's drifting continents would predict.

questions.question: Alfred Wegener noticed something obvious about a world map in 1912 — the bulge of Brazil seemed to fit into the notch of West Africa. What else did he assemble as evidence that the continents had once been joined?
questions.answer: Matching fossils of identical land animals and plants on both sides, plus matching rock layers and mountain belts
choices: Matching fossils of identical land animals and plants on both sides, plus matching rock layers and mountain belts
GPS readings showing the continents drifting apart at exactly two centimeters per year worldwide
Tide-gauge stations on either coast showing the Atlantic Ocean was getting visibly narrower
Sound recordings of the seafloor cracking, captured by Norwegian whaling-fleet hydrophones
questions.context: Wegener compiled Glossopteris fern fossils found in Africa, India, South America, Australia, and Antarctica; identical Mesosaurus reptile fossils in Brazil and South Africa; and Appalachian rocks matching Scottish Highlands strata. Geologists rejected his idea because he could not explain HOW continents moved through solid ocean floor.

questions.question: The Ring of Fire is the horseshoe-shaped belt around the Pacific Ocean where about 75% of the world's active volcanoes and most of its biggest earthquakes occur. What is happening geologically along this ring?
questions.answer: Dense oceanic plates are sliding under lighter continental plates, melting and triggering volcanism and quakes
choices: Dense oceanic plates are sliding under lighter continental plates, melting and triggering volcanism and quakes
A single underground river of magma circles the Pacific at constant depth and erupts at fixed intervals
Cold ocean water leaks down through cracks and chills the mantle, creating earthquake-prone weak zones
Ancient meteor impacts left a ring of shattered crust around the Pacific that still releases stored heat
questions.context: The Pacific Plate, Nazca Plate, Cocos Plate, and others are subducting (sliding under) the continental plates around them. Water carried down with the descending slab lowers the mantle's melting point, generating magma that rises to form volcanoes. The friction between locked plates builds up stress that releases as megathrust earthquakes — the 2011 Tohoku 9.1 and 1960 Chile 9.5 quakes were both ring-of-fire events.

questions.question: The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform boundary, meaning the Pacific and North American plates are not crashing into each other or pulling apart. What are they doing?
questions.answer: Sliding past each other horizontally, getting stuck for decades, then jerking forward as earthquakes
choices: Sliding past each other horizontally, getting stuck for decades, then jerking forward as earthquakes
Stacking up vertically against each other, raising the entire Sierra Nevada by inches every year
Pulling apart steadily so that California will be an island within the next fifty years
Rotating around a fixed central point near Los Angeles at about one degree per century
questions.context: Los Angeles is on the Pacific Plate moving northwest; San Francisco is on the North American Plate moving south relative to LA. The 1906 San Francisco quake (about magnitude 7.9) jumped the fault 20 feet horizontally in seconds. In tens of millions of years, LA will sit beside present-day San Francisco — not sink into the sea.

questions.question: Iceland sits directly on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which is why it has so many active volcanoes and geothermal hot springs. What's unusual about the geology underfoot for someone walking across Thingvellir National Park there?
questions.answer: You can literally walk between two continents, the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart on either side
choices: You can literally walk between two continents, the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart on either side
You can step on the geographic North Pole, marked permanently by a glacier that never melts there
You can stand on the same patch of rock that once sat exactly at Earth's equator in dinosaur times
You can hear underwater volcanoes from the rocks, since acoustic waves travel along the ridge
questions.context: Thingvellir (where the Vikings held the world's oldest parliament starting in 930 AD) lies in a rift valley where the two plates are spreading apart by about 2 cm per year. Tourists routinely photograph themselves with one hand on each continent. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is mostly underwater, but Iceland sits high enough on a volcanic hotspot that the ridge is visible above sea level.

questions.question: The Hawaiian Islands form a chain getting older from southeast to northwest — the Big Island has active volcanoes today, while Kauai's are extinct and eroded. What does this pattern reveal about how Hawaii formed?
questions.answer: A stationary hot spot in the mantle has been punching through the Pacific Plate as the plate drifts northwest
choices: A stationary hot spot in the mantle has been punching through the Pacific Plate as the plate drifts northwest
A meteor strike originally created the chain, with each island formed from a separate impact fragment
The islands all formed at once but eroded at different rates, with newer-looking ones simply being harder rock
Ancient coral reefs grew at different heights, and only the Big Island still has the right ocean temperature
questions.context: The Hawaiian hot spot has been roughly stationary for 80+ million years, while the Pacific Plate drifts northwest at about 7 cm per year. The chain bends near Midway because the plate's direction changed about 47 million years ago. Loihi, an underwater volcano southeast of the Big Island, will become the next Hawaiian island in tens of thousands of years.

questions.question: Mount Everest grew because the Indian Plate slammed into Asia about 50 million years ago and hasn't stopped pushing. What's still happening to the Himalayas today?
questions.answer: They are still rising about 5 mm per year as India keeps pushing under Asia, though erosion offsets most of the gain
choices: They are still rising about 5 mm per year as India keeps pushing under Asia, though erosion offsets most of the gain
They stopped growing 10 million years ago and are now shrinking faster than any other mountain range
They are tilting toward Tibet and will eventually collapse into the Indian Ocean as their base erodes
They grow only during earthquakes, with no measurable change in elevation between large seismic events
questions.context: The Indian Plate is still moving north at about 5 cm per year. GPS stations in the Himalayas detect uplift in real time. Marine fossils — corals and ammonites that lived on a Mesozoic sea floor — are found near the summit of Everest, evidence the rock was once seafloor. The Tibetan Plateau is the leading edge of this collision, lifted to an average elevation of 4,500 m.

questions.question: The Atlantic Ocean is getting wider, while the Pacific is shrinking. About how fast does the Atlantic widen each year, and how was this measured before satellites?
questions.answer: About 2.5 cm per year — the rate matched the magnetic-stripe widths recorded on the seafloor
choices: About 2.5 cm per year — the rate matched the magnetic-stripe widths recorded on the seafloor
About 2.5 m per year — measured by transatlantic cables stretching and snapping every few decades
About 2.5 km per year — measured by the gradual disappearance of small mid-Atlantic islands
About 2.5 mm per year — measured by tide-gauge stations on opposite coasts since the 1800s
questions.context: The Atlantic widens at fingernail-growth speed: about 2.5 cm per year averaged across the basin. Before GPS confirmed it directly in the 1990s, geologists already knew the rate from dated seafloor magnetic stripes — the width of each stripe divided by the duration of each known magnetic reversal gave the spreading rate. The Pacific's edges are subducting faster than the Atlantic widens, so the Pacific is slowly closing.

questions.question: Mount St. Helens erupted on May 18, 1980 with a sideways blast that flattened 230 square miles of forest. What kind of volcano is St. Helens, and why are these the most explosively dangerous?
questions.answer: A stratovolcano — its thick sticky magma traps gas pressure until catastrophic release, unlike runny basalt lava
choices: A stratovolcano — its thick sticky magma traps gas pressure until catastrophic release, unlike runny basalt lava
A shield volcano — its broad gentle slopes focus the eruption sideways instead of upward
A cinder cone volcano — its small size makes pressure buildup unavoidable in every single eruption
A submarine volcano — its proximity to water creates explosive steam blasts regardless of magma type
questions.context: Stratovolcanoes (composite volcanoes) build steep cones from alternating ash and lava layers and contain silica-rich magma that is viscous and gas-rich. Mount Fuji, Vesuvius, Pinatubo, and Krakatoa are all stratovolcanoes. Hawaiian shield volcanoes erupt much more quietly because their basaltic magma lets gas escape continuously.

questions.question: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia was the largest volcanic event in recorded history — about ten times Krakatoa's 1883 blast. What strange phenomenon did Europe and North America experience the following summer?
questions.answer: 1816 was 'the year without a summer' — snow fell in June, crops failed across Europe, and famine spread
choices: 1816 was 'the year without a summer' — snow fell in June, crops failed across Europe, and famine spread
1816 was the warmest summer on record — with European harvests doubling because of volcanic fertilizer ash
1816 saw the brightest auroras ever observed — visible as far south as Mexico and the Caribbean
1816 had no measurable weather impact — since Tambora was too distant to affect Northern Hemisphere climate
questions.context: Tambora ejected enough sulfur into the stratosphere to scatter sunlight worldwide for over a year. Mary Shelley was on holiday in Switzerland during the gloomy summer of 1816 and wrote Frankenstein indoors. New England saw snow in June. Crop failures triggered the last great European subsistence crisis and contributed to massive emigration to America.

questions.question: Yellowstone sits on top of a 'supervolcano' — a massive magma chamber under the park. The last full caldera eruption was about 640,000 years ago. What's the actual modern concern about it?
questions.answer: Geologists watch it but rate the near-term eruption risk as very low, most of the danger from Yellowstone today is hydrothermal explosions, not full caldera events
choices: Geologists watch it but rate the near-term eruption risk as very low, most of the danger from Yellowstone today is hydrothermal explosions, not full caldera events
It is scheduled to erupt within the next ten years according to US Geological Survey forecasting models
It already erupted in 2022 but the federal government suppressed the news to prevent panic responses
It cannot erupt again because the magma chamber drained completely during the previous caldera collapse
questions.context: The USGS monitors Yellowstone constantly. A full caldera event would be catastrophic continent-wide, but the probability per year is extremely small — roughly one in 700,000. Smaller hydrothermal blasts (like the 1989 Pork Chop Geyser event) happen frequently and are the real ongoing hazard for park visitors. Most media coverage exaggerates the imminent threat.

questions.question: Hawaiian volcanoes like Kilauea produce fluid lava flows that often look like glowing rivers, while volcanoes like Mount Vesuvius bury cities in ash and pyroclastic flows. The single biggest factor controlling this difference is what?
questions.answer: Magma viscosity, which depends on silica content — high-silica magma traps gas; low-silica magma flows freely
choices: Magma viscosity, which depends on silica content — high-silica magma traps gas; low-silica magma flows freely
Volcano height alone — since taller mountains always produce more violent eruptions than shorter ones
Local rainfall — since wetter regions automatically produce explosive steam-driven eruption styles
Magma temperature alone — since hotter magma is always more dangerous than cooler magma in every case
questions.context: Basaltic magma (low silica, ~50% SiO2) is hot and runny, letting gases escape continuously — Hawaiian-style. Andesitic and rhyolitic magma (high silica, 60-75%) is viscous and traps dissolved gases. When pressure releases, those gases expand explosively. Vesuvius, Pinatubo, and Mount St. Helens all erupted high-silica magma.

questions.question: Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79 AD, but not the way Hollywood often shows — lava did NOT flow down and engulf the city. What actually killed nearly everyone there?
questions.answer: Pyroclastic flows, superheated avalanches of ash, gas, and rock fragments racing downhill at hundreds of mph
choices: Pyroclastic flows, superheated avalanches of ash, gas, and rock fragments racing downhill at hundreds of mph
Slow lava streams that took several days to reach Pompeii while the residents tried to flee on foot
Underground methane explosions triggered by the eruption that destroyed buildings from below up
Tsunamis from the eruption that crossed the entire bay, and arrived just before the ashfall began
questions.context: Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and wrote two letters to Tacitus describing the eruption — the first eyewitness scientific account. The 'Plinian' eruption column collapsed several times, sending pyroclastic surges down the volcano at over 100 km/h with temperatures around 250°C. The famous plaster casts at Pompeii are voids left by victims' bodies in the compacted ash.

questions.question: The Richter scale was developed by Charles Richter in 1935 to measure earthquake size, but seismologists today usually use the 'moment magnitude' scale instead for large quakes. Why was Richter replaced?
questions.answer: Richter saturates above magnitude 7, it cannot distinguish a magnitude 8 from a magnitude 9, while moment magnitude can
choices: Richter saturates above magnitude 7, it cannot distinguish a magnitude 8 from a magnitude 9, while moment magnitude can
Richter only worked in Southern California, and gives wrong readings for earthquakes anywhere else
Richter was banned by the United Nations after being misused during political disputes over disaster aid
Richter was never accurate, and his original 1935 paper was retracted in the late 1980s for methodology issues
questions.context: Charles Richter designed his scale using a specific seismometer for shallow Southern California quakes. The scale works for small-to-moderate earthquakes but loses sensitivity at large magnitudes because the assumed wave behavior breaks down. Moment magnitude (Mw, developed by Tom Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori in 1979) measures the energy released by the fault slip directly and remains valid at any size.

questions.question: The 2011 Tohoku earthquake off Japan was a magnitude 9.1, which sounds only slightly bigger than a magnitude 8.1. In actual energy released, how much bigger was it?
questions.answer: About 32 times more energy — the magnitude scale is logarithmic, so each whole number is ~32× more energy
choices: About 32 times more energy — the magnitude scale is logarithmic, so each whole number is ~32× more energy
About twice as much energy — the magnitude scale is a simple linear ratio between sizes of earthquakes
About 10 times more energy — every whole magnitude exactly multiplies the energy by ten, by definition
About 100 times more energy — the magnitude scale doubles the energy for each tenth of a unit increase
questions.context: Each unit increase on the moment magnitude scale represents roughly a 32× increase in energy release (it's a 10× increase in ground-motion amplitude, but energy goes as amplitude to the 3/2 power). A magnitude 9 releases about 1,000× the energy of a magnitude 7. The 2004 Sumatra (9.1) and 2011 Tohoku (9.1) quakes were among the most energetic events ever recorded.

questions.question: When a megathrust earthquake happens at a subduction zone, the seafloor can jump upward by meters in seconds. What deadly secondary hazard does this generate, and how fast does it travel in deep ocean?
questions.answer: A tsunami — moving in open ocean at jet-airliner speeds of around 800 km/h, slowing as it approaches shore
choices: A tsunami — moving in open ocean at jet-airliner speeds of around 800 km/h, slowing as it approaches shore
A storm surge — pushed by the wind from the same low-pressure system that triggered the quake activity
A sea-level drop — caused by the suction of the falling seafloor pulling water toward the open ocean center
A magnetic anomaly — the disturbance scrambles ship compasses but does no other physical harm to coasts
questions.context: Tsunamis travel at about sqrt(g × depth) — in 4 km deep ocean, that's about 700-800 km/h, faster than most airliners. In open water the wave height is small (often a meter or less), making tsunamis nearly invisible from a ship. They pile up dramatically only when they reach shallow coastal water. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed ~230,000 across 14 countries; the 2011 Tohoku tsunami killed ~19,500 in Japan.

questions.question: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile was the most powerful ever measured, at moment magnitude 9.5. Beyond the immediate Chilean coast, what happened across the Pacific that day?
questions.answer: Tsunamis crossed the entire ocean, killing people in Hawaii ~15 hours later and Japan ~22 hours later
choices: Tsunamis crossed the entire ocean, killing people in Hawaii ~15 hours later and Japan ~22 hours later
The earthquake stopped at the Chilean border, and had no measurable Pacific-basin effect at all
Auroras lit up over Australia from the geomagnetic disturbance the quake created in the upper atmosphere
Submarine cables across the Pacific broke simultaneously, but only the Chilean coastline saw any waves
questions.context: The Valdivia quake released energy roughly equivalent to 4,500 atomic bombs. Tsunami waves up to 10 m struck Hawaii's Hilo Bay 15 hours later, killing 61 people, then reached Japan ~22 hours after the quake, killing 142 more. The disaster led to the establishment of the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center in Hawaii (1965).

questions.question: Most people know about the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago, but Earth has had five major mass extinctions. Which one — known as 'the Great Dying' — was actually the worst, and when?
questions.answer: The Permian-Triassic extinction about 252 million years ago, which killed roughly 95% of marine species
choices: The Permian-Triassic extinction about 252 million years ago, which killed roughly 95% of marine species
The Pleistocene Ice Age extinction about 12,000 years ago, killing all of the giant Australian marsupials
The Cambrian extinction about 540 million years ago, killing the famous early Burgess Shale fauna types
The Holocene extinction event of the year 1850, killing roughly half of all known plant species globally
questions.context: The Permian-Triassic extinction wiped out about 95% of marine species and 70% of terrestrial vertebrate species. The likely cause was massive volcanism in the Siberian Traps — eruptions that released CO2, sulfur, and methane over hundreds of thousands of years. Life took 5-10 million years to recover diversity. Modern paleontologists call it the worst biological catastrophe in Earth's history.

questions.question: Father-and-son physicists Luis and Walter Alvarez published in 1980 that an asteroid killed the dinosaurs. What was the specific physical evidence they used to make their case?
questions.answer: A thin worldwide clay layer at the K-T boundary rich in iridium, an element rare on Earth but abundant in asteroids
choices: A thin worldwide clay layer at the K-T boundary rich in iridium, an element rare on Earth but abundant in asteroids
Carbon-dated dinosaur bones showing all known species died within exactly the same calendar year
Egyptian temple carvings depicting a fireball striking the Yucatan and ending the age of giant lizards
Volcanic ash layers in Antarctica that matched no known terrestrial volcano of the right time period
questions.context: Luis Alvarez (Nobel-winning physicist) and his son Walter (geologist) found iridium enrichment in the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary clay layer worldwide. Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in meteorites. The crater they predicted was confirmed in 1991 — the Chicxulub crater off Mexico's Yucatan peninsula, ~180 km across and 66 million years old. The asteroid was about 10 km wide.

questions.question: The Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago threw enough debris into the atmosphere to block sunlight for years. Why did this kill non-avian dinosaurs but spare most mammals and birds?
questions.answer: Small body size let mammals survive in burrows and on a few insects; collapsing food webs hit large herbivores hardest
choices: Small body size let mammals survive in burrows and on a few insects; collapsing food webs hit large herbivores hardest
Mammals had developed fur for warmth, while dinosaurs were universally cold-blooded and froze immediately
Mammals lived only in deep caves and were therefore shielded from the impact's initial heat-pulse wave
Mammals had immunity to the radiation released by the impact, while all dinosaurs were highly susceptible
questions.context: Modern paleontology shows many dinosaurs were warm-blooded and feathered; birds ARE dinosaurs (avian dinosaurs survived). The kill mechanism was ecosystem collapse: photosynthesis crashed, large herbivores starved, large carnivores followed, food chains dependent on living plants collapsed top-to-bottom. Mammals at the time were mostly small, omnivorous, and burrow-living — perfect survivors for a years-long dark winter feeding on detritus and insects.

questions.question: There were five 'Big Five' mass extinctions in Earth's deep past — the Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, and Cretaceous. Was each one caused by an asteroid impact?
questions.answer: No — only the Cretaceous is confidently linked to an asteroid; others involved volcanism, anoxia, or glaciation
choices: No — only the Cretaceous is confidently linked to an asteroid; others involved volcanism, anoxia, or glaciation
Yes — every mass extinction in Earth history has been confirmed as caused by an asteroid impact event
Yes — but each impact was a moon-sized object, and the kill mechanism was always the tidal disruption that followed
No — every mass extinction except the dinosaur one was caused by humans hunting megafauna to extinction
questions.context: The Big Five: Ordovician-Silurian (~444 Mya, glaciation-driven sea-level drop), Late Devonian (~372 Mya, ocean anoxia), Permian-Triassic (~252 Mya, Siberian Traps volcanism), Triassic-Jurassic (~201 Mya, Central Atlantic Magmatic Province volcanism), Cretaceous-Paleogene (~66 Mya, Chicxulub asteroid plus possibly Deccan Traps volcanism). Each had distinct causes — there's no single mechanism behind all extinctions.

questions.question: About 250 million years ago a massive flood-basalt eruption in what is now Siberia covered an area the size of Australia in lava. Why do many geologists link this to the Permian extinction?
questions.answer: The eruption released CO2, sulfur, and methane over hundreds of thousands of years, acidifying oceans and warming climate severely
choices: The eruption released CO2, sulfur, and methane over hundreds of thousands of years, acidifying oceans and warming climate severely
The eruption physically buried 95% of marine species under solid lava and prevented any escape route at all
The eruption created a permanent volcanic winter that lasted 10 million years and froze all of the oceans solid
The eruption opened the magnetic field to deadly cosmic radiation that immediately killed all surface life forms
questions.context: The Siberian Traps formed from a flood-basalt event that lasted ~1 million years and released enormous quantities of greenhouse gases plus sulfur aerosols. Marine sediments show severe ocean anoxia (oxygen loss) and acidification at the boundary. Multiple kill mechanisms operating together — heat, acid, anoxia, ozone depletion — explain why the Permian event was so severe.

questions.question: John Tyndall in 1859 set up a brass tube with infrared radiation passing through it, then tested which gases blocked the heat. What did he find about ordinary nitrogen and oxygen versus carbon dioxide and water vapor?
questions.answer: Nitrogen and oxygen are nearly transparent to infrared; CO2 and water vapor absorb it strongly — the basis of the greenhouse effect
choices: Nitrogen and oxygen are nearly transparent to infrared; CO2 and water vapor absorb it strongly — the basis of the greenhouse effect
All gases absorb infrared equally — there is no special role for carbon dioxide in atmospheric heating
Carbon dioxide is transparent to infrared while oxygen blocks it — the opposite of the modern textbook claim
Only water vapor absorbs infrared — and CO2 has no measurable greenhouse effect even at high concentrations
questions.context: Tyndall's 1859 experiment is the foundational measurement underlying the greenhouse effect. Svante Arrhenius extended the work in 1896 to calculate how much warming a doubling of CO2 might produce. The basic physics is firmly established. What remains contested at the policy level is climate sensitivity (how much warming per doubling, including feedbacks), cloud effects, and what humans should do — not the IR-absorption property itself.

questions.question: Earth's climate today is often compared to its past, but reconstructions show several past warm periods even before factories existed. What is the Medieval Warm Period, and what kind of evidence supports it?
questions.answer: A warm interval roughly 950-1250 AD when Vikings farmed Greenland and grapes grew in England, recorded in tree rings, ice cores, and historical documents
choices: A warm interval roughly 950-1250 AD when Vikings farmed Greenland and grapes grew in England, recorded in tree rings, ice cores, and historical documents
A future warming projected in IPCC models that has not yet occurred but is expected by the end of the century
A regional myth from European folklore with no actual physical or documentary evidence supporting it
A brief warm spell during the 1500s caused by sunspot activity at the very end of the Renaissance period
questions.context: The MWP (~950-1250 AD) is documented in tree-ring proxies, lake-sediment records, and historical evidence: Norse settlement of Greenland (985 AD, abandoned ~1450 as cooling returned), English vineyards reaching as far north as Yorkshire, abundant Mediterranean harvest records. The IPCC's earlier 'hockey stick' graph (Mann et al. 1998) downplayed the MWP, but updated reconstructions including those from CRU and Lamb's original work recognize it as a real Northern Hemisphere phenomenon at minimum.

questions.question: From roughly 1300 to 1850 the world cooled into what's called the Little Ice Age. What dramatic everyday-life evidence in London tells us about this period?
questions.answer: The Thames River froze solid enough to hold 'frost fairs' on the ice, with markets, fires, and bull-baiting
choices: The Thames River froze solid enough to hold 'frost fairs' on the ice, with markets, fires, and bull-baiting
London received its very first snowfall in recorded history during this period of unusually warm weather
Citrus fruit groves spread north of London for the first time, replacing the previous local wheat farming
The Thames River became so warm tropical fish were caught in it, suggesting volcanic heating from below
questions.context: Frost fairs on the frozen Thames are recorded from 1607 onward, the most famous in 1683-84. Mountain glaciers in the Alps and Norway advanced and overran villages. The 'Year Without a Summer' (1816, after the Tambora eruption) fell within the LIA's later phase. Painters of the period — Avercamp, Bruegel — show snowy scenes that match the cool-climate evidence. Crop failures fed political instability across Europe.

questions.question: The Maunder Minimum (~1645-1715) was a long stretch during which astronomers observed almost no sunspots on the Sun. What's the suspected link between this and the Little Ice Age weather of the same time?
questions.answer: Reduced solar activity coincided with the LIA's coldest decades — suggesting solar variation contributes to Earth's climate
choices: Reduced solar activity coincided with the LIA's coldest decades — suggesting solar variation contributes to Earth's climate
Increased solar activity heated the upper atmosphere — pushing all the surface heat down into the oceans
Sunspots have no climate effect of any kind — the timing of the Maunder Minimum was pure coincidence
Increased solar flares triggered massive volcanic eruptions on Earth — and the volcanoes caused all the cooling
questions.context: Edward Maunder (and Spörer before him) noted the near-disappearance of sunspots between roughly 1645 and 1715, despite improving telescopes. The 11-year solar cycle nearly flatlined. This overlapped with the coldest decades of the LIA. Solar irradiance varies only ~0.1% over the cycle, so the magnitude of any direct effect is debated — but reconstructions using solar proxies (beryllium-10 in ice cores) confirm low solar activity during cool periods.

questions.question: Serbian astronomer Milutin Milankovitch in the 1920s proposed that Earth's ice ages follow a predictable astronomical pattern. What does his theory blame for the timing of glacial advances?
questions.answer: Tiny variations in Earth's orbit shape, axial tilt, and wobble — together changing where sunlight falls on the planet over thousands of years
choices: Tiny variations in Earth's orbit shape, axial tilt, and wobble — together changing where sunlight falls on the planet over thousands of years
Cycles of volcanic eruption that follow a 100,000-year clock — building up over time and then releasing all at once
Variations in the speed of light reaching Earth from distant galaxies — increasing or decreasing surface warming
Periodic shifts in the magnetic poles of Earth — flipping every few thousand years and disrupting all climate patterns
questions.context: Milankovitch identified three cycles: eccentricity (~100,000 years), obliquity/axial tilt (~41,000 years), and precession (~26,000 years). The combination changes how much summer sunlight reaches high northern latitudes — where ice-age ice sheets grow or shrink. Deep-sea sediment cores and ice-core data from the 1970s onward confirmed his predictions. Glacial cycles since the early Pleistocene fit his pattern, with significant amplification from CO2 feedbacks.

questions.question: Plants need CO2 to grow — it's the carbon in photosynthesis. Satellite observations since the 1980s have measured a striking change in global vegetation. What is it?
questions.answer: Earth's vegetated area has 'greened' by ~5% since 1980, with CO2 fertilization estimated to drive much of the gain
choices: Earth's vegetated area has 'greened' by ~5% since 1980, with CO2 fertilization estimated to drive much of the gain
Earth's vegetated area has shrunk by ~5% since 1980, mostly because of CO2-driven heat damage to crops
Earth's vegetated area has not changed in any measurable way since the very first NASA satellites launched
Earth's vegetated area has doubled since 1980 because all of the deserts have become tropical rainforests
questions.context: Studies using MODIS and AVHRR satellite data (Zhu et al. 2016 in Nature Climate Change, and follow-up work) document significant 'global greening.' CO2 fertilization is estimated to account for most of the gain, with land-use change and nitrogen deposition contributing. The greening doesn't refute climate change concerns — it does complicate single-narrative framings. Crop yields globally have grown alongside rising CO2.

questions.question: The basic physics of CO2 as a greenhouse gas is firmly established (Tyndall, Arrhenius). Why does that fact not by itself settle the climate-policy debate?
questions.answer: Knowing CO2 absorbs IR doesn't reveal the magnitude of warming, feedback effects, or what the right policy response is
choices: Knowing CO2 absorbs IR doesn't reveal the magnitude of warming, feedback effects, or what the right policy response is
Tyndall's experiment was never reproduced, so the basic physics is actually as uncertain as the policy questions
CO2 only absorbs IR at high temperatures, so it doesn't matter for ordinary surface temperatures at all
The physics matters only for the upper atmosphere, where humans have no policy interest of any practical kind
questions.context: Climate sensitivity (warming per doubling of CO2, including feedbacks) is estimated between roughly 1.5 and 4.5°C in the IPCC literature — a range that hasn't tightened much in 40 years. Cloud feedbacks remain the largest uncertainty. Beyond the science, there's a separate set of questions: how fast warming proceeds, what humans should do, who pays, and what tradeoffs are worth it. Steven Koonin's *Unsettled* (2021) develops this distinction.

questions.question: Hurricane formation requires several specific conditions, which is why hurricanes don't form just anywhere. What's the minimum ocean surface temperature usually needed for tropical-cyclone formation?
questions.answer: About 26.5°C (~80°F) over a deep layer of warm water — colder oceans starve the storm of evaporated water vapor
choices: About 26.5°C (~80°F) over a deep layer of warm water — colder oceans starve the storm of evaporated water vapor
About 4°C (~39°F) — hurricanes form in cold water and gain energy from the temperature gradient with land
Any temperature above freezing — hurricane formation depends entirely on wind patterns, not on water temperature
Exactly the temperature of human blood (~37°C) — a coincidence noted by mariners since the eighteenth century
questions.context: Hurricanes also need low vertical wind shear, sufficient Coriolis force (so they don't form within ~5° of the equator), atmospheric instability, and a pre-existing disturbance. The 26.5°C threshold is approximate — the real driver is the energy available from evaporation. The Atlantic basin's hurricane season peaks in August-October when sea surface temperatures are highest. The Pacific has typhoons; the Indian Ocean has cyclones; the storm is the same kind of system.

questions.question: In 1985 British Antarctic Survey scientists Farman, Gardiner, and Shanklin published in *Nature* their measurement of a dramatic ozone hole over Antarctica each spring. What chemical caused it, and what was done?
questions.answer: CFCs from refrigerators and aerosol sprays — phased out worldwide by the 1987 Montreal Protocol, with ozone now recovering
choices: CFCs from refrigerators and aerosol sprays — phased out worldwide by the 1987 Montreal Protocol, with ozone now recovering
Coal smoke from power plants — phased out by the Kyoto Protocol of 1997 with mixed regional results
Volcanic sulfur from Mount Pinatubo — which simply self-corrected once the volcano stopped erupting in 1991
Carbon dioxide from industry — which the Montreal Protocol addressed alongside the regular ozone problem
questions.context: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland predicted in 1974 that CFCs would deplete ozone. Paul Crutzen identified the role of nitrogen oxides. The three shared the 1995 Nobel in Chemistry. The Montreal Protocol (signed Sept 1987) phased out CFCs globally — one of the most successful environmental treaties ever. The Antarctic ozone hole is now slowly closing; full recovery is expected by ~2070. A genuine environmental success story driven by clear science and international cooperation.

questions.question: The Montreal Protocol is widely cited as the most successful environmental treaty ever signed. What feature made compliance practical for industry in a way that later climate agreements have struggled to match?
questions.answer: Chemists had ready alternatives to CFCs (HFCs, HCFCs) at similar cost, so the transition was technically feasible
choices: Chemists had ready alternatives to CFCs (HFCs, HCFCs) at similar cost, so the transition was technically feasible
Industry agreed to absorb unlimited compliance costs without any technical alternative ever being developed
Governments declared CFCs illegal worldwide overnight, with no industry adjustment period of any kind
Consumers stopped using refrigeration and air conditioning voluntarily after public education campaigns
questions.context: Replacement chemicals (HFCs, HCFCs) were available and the costs of conversion were affordable for refrigerant manufacturers. The Kigali Amendment (2016) extended Montreal to phase down HFCs themselves, which turned out to be potent greenhouse gases. The contrast with energy-system decarbonization is instructive: replacing fossil fuels with low-carbon energy at similar cost across the entire economy is much harder than swapping one refrigerant chemical for another.

questions.question: The ozone layer protects Earth's surface from harmful ultraviolet radiation. Why is ozone protective when ordinary oxygen (the O2 we breathe) isn't?
questions.answer: Ozone (O3) has a triple-atom structure that absorbs UV-B at specific wavelengths that pass right through O2
choices: Ozone (O3) has a triple-atom structure that absorbs UV-B at specific wavelengths that pass right through O2
Ozone is heavier than oxygen and acts as a simple physical shield, like a thick blanket above the planet
Ozone reflects sunlight back into space like a mirror, so cooler UV simply never reaches the lower atmosphere
Ozone has no protective role, the protection comes entirely from nitrogen in the stratosphere itself
questions.context: UV photons in the 240-310 nm range break O3 apart, then the products recombine — a continuous cycle that absorbs UV energy without permanently depleting ozone (unless catalysts like chlorine from CFCs accelerate the breakdown). Without the ozone layer, UV-B reaching Earth's surface would dramatically increase skin cancer, eye damage, and harm to marine plankton at the base of the food chain. Stratospheric ozone is a thin layer concentrated about 15-35 km up.

questions.question: In late 1609 Galileo Galilei pointed his improved telescope at Jupiter and saw four small points of light. What did he realize about them over the following nights?
questions.answer: They moved with Jupiter night after night, they were moons orbiting another planet, not Earth, undermining Earth-centered cosmology
choices: They moved with Jupiter night after night, they were moons orbiting another planet, not Earth, undermining Earth-centered cosmology
They were fixed stars behind Jupiter that simply happened to be in line with the planet that month
They were Galileo's own eye floaters reflected in the telescope lens, an artifact of poor optics
They were Jupiter's moons but in retrograde orbits, orbiting Earth while also surrounding Jupiter
questions.context: Galileo named the four moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto) the 'Medicean stars' after his patron Cosimo de' Medici; we now call them the Galilean moons. Their orbit around Jupiter directly contradicted the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic view that everything circled the Earth. He published in *Sidereus Nuncius* (March 1610). The Catholic Church accepted this finding initially — the real conflict came later with heliocentrism.

questions.question: Galileo's telescope showed that Venus goes through 'phases' like the Moon — sometimes crescent, sometimes nearly full, sometimes gibbous. Why does this observation specifically refute Ptolemy's Earth-centered universe?
questions.answer: Venus shows a full set of phases only if it orbits the Sun — Ptolemy's geocentric model couldn't produce a full or gibbous Venus
choices: Venus shows a full set of phases only if it orbits the Sun — Ptolemy's geocentric model couldn't produce a full or gibbous Venus
Venus shouldn't have phases at all — Ptolemy specifically predicted that planets never change appearance over time
Phases would mean Venus is bigger than Earth — and Ptolemy claimed it was much smaller than all of the Moon
Galileo's observations were illusions caused by the telescope lens — they don't actually disprove Ptolemy at all
questions.context: In Ptolemy's geocentric model, Venus's epicycle kept it between Earth and the Sun, so it could only show crescent phases — never gibbous or full. Galileo's 1610 observation of a nearly-full Venus was direct evidence Venus passes behind the Sun, requiring a heliocentric arrangement. Tycho Brahe's hybrid model could accommodate the phases, but Ptolemy's pure geocentrism could not. Galileo published this in *Letters on Sunspots* (1613).

questions.question: Isaac Newton's *Principia Mathematica* in 1687 unified the falling apple in his garden with the orbiting Moon. What was Newton's actual insight that connected them?
questions.answer: The same gravity that pulls the apple downward also holds the Moon in its orbit — a universal force acting on all matter
choices: The same gravity that pulls the apple downward also holds the Moon in its orbit — a universal force acting on all matter
Apples fall because of magnetism — the same force that holds the Moon in orbit around the Earth
The Moon does not orbit Earth — it is held in place by air pressure trapped above the atmosphere
Gravity only operates on living matter, like the apple — the Moon is held by a different physical force
questions.context: Newton's *Principia* introduced the inverse-square law of universal gravitation (F = G m1 m2 / r²), the three laws of motion, and the calculus needed to derive Kepler's planetary orbits from those laws. Edmund Halley funded the publication. The unification of celestial and terrestrial physics was perhaps the single most important shift in scientific worldview — heaven and earth, suddenly, were governed by the same equations.

questions.question: The Hubble Deep Field image (1995) showed about 3,000 galaxies in a tiny patch of sky that astronomers had thought was nearly empty. What did this reveal about the universe?
questions.answer: Almost every dark patch of sky is packed with distant galaxies — the universe contains hundreds of billions of them
choices: Almost every dark patch of sky is packed with distant galaxies — the universe contains hundreds of billions of them
The visible universe contains exactly 3,000 galaxies in total — fewer than astronomers had previously estimated
Dark patches of sky are truly empty — and the 3,000 objects in the Hubble image were optical artifacts
Galaxies cluster only along narrow lines visible from Earth — most other directions are completely empty
questions.context: Robert Williams, then Hubble Space Telescope Institute director, gambled his director's discretionary time on a 10-day exposure of an apparently empty patch of sky in Ursa Major. The image showed thousands of galaxies, many faint and red-shifted from the early universe. The Hubble Ultra Deep Field (2004) went deeper still. James Webb Space Telescope (launched 2021, operational 2022) sees even further back, finding galaxies that formed when the universe was only ~300 million years old.

questions.question: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched on December 25, 2021 and operates about 1.5 million km from Earth at the L2 Lagrange point. Why is it observing in infrared, not visible light like Hubble?
questions.answer: Light from the earliest galaxies has been red-shifted into the infrared by cosmic expansion — invisible to Hubble's optical eye
choices: Light from the earliest galaxies has been red-shifted into the infrared by cosmic expansion — invisible to Hubble's optical eye
Visible light cannot travel through the empty vacuum of deep space — only infrared can make the long journey
JWST's mirrors are too cold to detect visible light at any wavelength — they can only register heat radiation
Hubble's visible-light data was complete — and there was nothing left to discover with that wavelength range
questions.context: Cosmological redshift stretches the wavelengths of photons traveling across an expanding universe. Light emitted as visible by a galaxy 13 billion years ago arrives at Earth shifted into infrared. JWST's 6.5 m primary mirror (made of 18 gold-coated beryllium hexagons) captures this infrared with extraordinary sensitivity. JWST has already found galaxies hundreds of millions of years older than Hubble could detect.

questions.question: Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times in geological history, with north and south poles trading places. Where is the clearest record of these reversals preserved?
questions.answer: In magnetic-stripe patterns on the seafloor, where new ocean crust records the field's direction as it cools
choices: In magnetic-stripe patterns on the seafloor, where new ocean crust records the field's direction as it cools
In tree-ring patterns, where the direction of cell growth tracks the magnetic field of each year
In oral histories from Pacific Islanders, who passed down stories of compass-needle reversals for centuries
In the metal of dinosaur bones, which preserved the magnetic alignment of their living tissues at death
questions.context: The Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis (1963) identified seafloor magnetic stripes as a tape recording of Earth's magnetic-field reversals. Iron-rich minerals in fresh seafloor lava lock in the field's current direction as they cool. The most recent reversal — the Brunhes-Matuyama — happened about 780,000 years ago. The next one isn't predictable in detail but is overdue by long-term averages; the magnetic-pole drift in recent decades has been unusually fast.

questions.question: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place in the ocean — Challenger Deep reaches about 10,935 m. What's happening geologically that makes such trenches form?
questions.answer: An oceanic plate is being subducted under another plate — plunging down into the mantle at a steep angle
choices: An oceanic plate is being subducted under another plate — plunging down into the mantle at a steep angle
Hot mantle rock is rising upward — and creating a low spot where the surface has not yet caught up
An ancient meteor impact left a deep crater that the ocean later filled — the deepest known on Earth
Underground rivers eroded the sea bottom for millions of years — carving deep channels in the seafloor
questions.context: At the Mariana Trench, the Pacific Plate is subducting under the smaller Mariana Plate. The plates bend down sharply, creating the trench. James Cameron's Deepsea Challenger sub reached Challenger Deep in 2012 — only the third manned descent (after Trieste in 1960). Subducted material carries surface water and sediment deep into the mantle, helping drive volcanism above.

questions.question: About 24,000 years ago, ice sheets nearly two miles thick covered most of Canada and parts of the northern US. The 1837 work of Swiss naturalist Louis Agassiz proposed something controversial about this. What was it?
questions.answer: That Earth had repeatedly entered and exited 'ice ages' — periods when massive glaciers reshaped continents
choices: That Earth had repeatedly entered and exited 'ice ages' — periods when massive glaciers reshaped continents
That the Biblical Flood had been an ice flood — covering the world with ice rather than liquid water
That glaciers grew only in the Alps and never in North America — despite reports from American geologists
That ice never melts naturally — only volcanic activity can end an ice age once one has begun on Earth
questions.context: Agassiz proposed his 'ice age' theory in 1837 after studying erratic boulders, moraines, and U-shaped valleys in the Alps. The scientific establishment was skeptical for years — biblical flood narratives competed with the deep-time picture. Field evidence eventually overwhelmed the resistance. Modern paleoclimate work identifies many Pleistocene glaciations on Milankovitch cycles, with shorter Quaternary ice ages and longer periods of warmth between.

questions.question: Modern volcanoes are dramatic but small compared to ancient 'large igneous provinces' that erupted millions of cubic km of basalt over short geological times. What is the Deccan Traps in India?
questions.answer: A vast flood-basalt province that erupted around 66 million years ago, possibly contributing to the dinosaur extinction
choices: A vast flood-basalt province that erupted around 66 million years ago, possibly contributing to the dinosaur extinction
A modern Indian volcano range that erupts once per century with predictable timing, and impact
A network of underground rivers in central India that drains the entire subcontinent's monsoon water
A mountain range built entirely by the collision of India with Asia about 50 million years ago
questions.context: The Deccan Traps cover about 500,000 square km of western India in basalt up to 2 km thick. Eruptions span roughly 66 million years ago — overlapping the Chicxulub impact. Some paleontologists argue the dinosaur extinction was a combined event: the impact delivered the killing blow but climate-disrupting Deccan volcanism had already stressed ecosystems. Others assign the extinction primarily to the asteroid.

questions.question: Coastal glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica calve massive icebergs that drift away into the ocean. What process actually controls how fast these ice sheets lose mass overall, separate from melting?
questions.answer: Iceberg calving — and submarine melting at the glacier face account for roughly half of total ice-sheet mass loss
choices: Iceberg calving — and submarine melting at the glacier face account for roughly half of total ice-sheet mass loss
Surface melting accounts for 100% of ice loss — calving is just for show and adds nothing to net loss
Wind erosion of ice surfaces drives all ice loss — water-related processes are too slow to be significant
Ice sheets do not lose mass overall — they grow continuously through ongoing precipitation each year
questions.context: For both Greenland and Antarctica, dynamic mass loss (icebergs breaking off, ice flowing into the sea faster) is comparable in magnitude to surface melting. The Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers in West Antarctica are watched closely because they sit on bedrock below sea level — warm ocean water can melt them from below. Greenland loses about 280 billion tons per year on recent averages.

questions.question: Earth has had at least one 'snowball Earth' episode in the deep past — possibly several — when ice may have covered the planet from pole to pole. When did the most severe likely occur?
questions.answer: Around 700 million years ago, in the Cryogenian period — based on glacial deposits found at then-tropical latitudes
choices: Around 700 million years ago, in the Cryogenian period — based on glacial deposits found at then-tropical latitudes
Around 12,000 years ago — at the end of the most recent ice age that humans actually lived through
Around 65 million years ago — at the same time the dinosaurs went extinct from the Chicxulub impact
Around 4.5 billion years ago — when the Earth first formed and was still cooling from initial molten state
questions.context: Joseph Kirschvink coined 'snowball Earth' in 1992 based on Neoproterozoic glacial deposits found in equatorial regions (when the continents are reconstructed to their then-positions). The Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations both appear to have been global. CO2 from volcanism eventually accumulated enough to break the ice-albedo feedback, then drove rapid warming. The episodes preceded the Cambrian explosion of complex life.

questions.question: The Cambrian explosion (~540 million years ago) was a sudden geological-blink appearance of nearly all major animal body plans. What's the strange feature that puzzled Darwin himself?
questions.answer: The fossil record below the Cambrian was almost empty of complex animals, apparently jumping from microbes to diverse fauna
choices: The fossil record below the Cambrian was almost empty of complex animals, apparently jumping from microbes to diverse fauna
The Cambrian fossils were perfectly preserved while all other periods had only partial remains worldwide
The Cambrian appeared in a single small region of Wales, Darwin couldn't explain why no other location had fossils
The Cambrian fossils were all of one species, Darwin couldn't explain why diversity then collapsed afterward
questions.context: Darwin admitted in *On the Origin of Species* that the apparent suddenness of the Cambrian explosion was a difficulty for his gradualist theory. Modern paleontology has found Ediacaran biota (~575-541 Mya) and earlier — there's a Precambrian record, just thin. Triggers for the Cambrian event are debated: oxygen rises, predator-prey coevolution, calcium availability, Snowball-Earth recovery, and developmental-genetic changes are all candidates.

questions.question: Comets sometimes have spectacularly long tails that always point away from the Sun, regardless of which direction the comet is moving. What pushes the tail?
questions.answer: Solar wind, and radiation pressure from sunlight push comet gas and dust away from the Sun
choices: Solar wind, and radiation pressure from sunlight push comet gas and dust away from the Sun
The comet's own forward motion drags the tail backward, like exhaust behind a moving car
Earth's gravity pulls the tail in our direction whenever the comet is closer than Mars
Magnetism between the comet, and Sun creates an attractive force that pulls the tail outward
questions.context: Comets have two tails: a curved dust tail (pushed by solar radiation pressure) and a straight ion tail (pushed by the solar wind). Both point away from the Sun, which is why a comet's tail leads it on its outbound journey. Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years (next visible 2061). Comet Hale-Bopp in 1997 had a tail visible to the naked eye for weeks.

questions.question: Two NASA Voyager spacecraft launched in 1977 are still transmitting data from interstellar space after almost half a century. What's the major engineering achievement that lets them keep working so far away?
questions.answer: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) using plutonium-238, converting nuclear decay heat into electricity for decades
choices: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) using plutonium-238, converting nuclear decay heat into electricity for decades
Solar panels that grew to compensate as the Sun became more distant during their long outward journey
Energy beamed wirelessly from Earth via dedicated transmitters operating continuously since 1977
Hibernation cycles in which the spacecraft turn off completely between rare data transmissions back to Earth
questions.context: RTGs powered both Voyagers from launch through today. Plutonium-238 has a half-life of about 87 years, decaying to uranium-234 and releasing heat that thermocouples convert to electricity. The power output drops slowly over time; NASA has progressively turned off non-essential instruments. Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and is now ~24 billion km from Earth. The Golden Records aboard each carry sounds and images of Earth.

questions.question: Black holes were once a purely theoretical curiosity from Einstein's general relativity. What changed in April 2019 to make them photographable for the first time?
questions.answer: The Event Horizon Telescope used a network of radio dishes across continents to image M87's central black hole
choices: The Event Horizon Telescope used a network of radio dishes across continents to image M87's central black hole
A new Hubble Space Telescope camera could see directly inside an event horizon for the very first time
A nearby supernova illuminated a previously invisible black hole near Earth's solar system for a few hours
Black holes were proven not to exist, and the April 2019 image showed only ordinary stars at the location
questions.context: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration linked radio dishes from Hawaii to Spain to Antarctica into a virtual Earth-sized telescope. The April 2019 image showed the bright accretion ring around M87*, a supermassive black hole 53 million light-years away with mass of about 6.5 billion suns. A 2022 EHT image showed Sagittarius A*, our own galaxy's central black hole (~4 million solar masses). Both confirm Einstein's predictions in extreme gravity regimes.

questions.question: In 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs were trying to clean up static in their radio antenna, even sweeping pigeon droppings out of the horn. What did they accidentally discover?
questions.answer: The cosmic microwave background — the leftover heat-glow from the Big Bang, filling the entire universe
choices: The cosmic microwave background — the leftover heat-glow from the Big Bang, filling the entire universe
Radio signals from alien civilizations — confirmed by the SETI Institute later in 1965 as artificial
Earth's natural magnetic-field hum — which they patented and licensed to AT&T for telecommunications
Background radio noise from solar flares — which they showed varied with the eleven-year sunspot cycle
questions.context: Penzias and Wilson found a 3 K microwave signal coming from every direction equally — and after eliminating known sources (including pigeons in the horn), realized it matched a theoretical prediction by Gamow, Alpher, and Herman in the 1940s that the early universe should have left a cosmic microwave background. The signal had been hypothesized but never observed. They shared the 1978 Nobel in Physics with Pyotr Kapitsa.

questions.question: Edwin Hubble in 1929 announced that distant galaxies are receding from us — and the farther they are, the faster they recede. What did this discovery imply about the universe?
questions.answer: The universe is expanding — extrapolating backward gave the first observational evidence for the Big Bang
choices: The universe is expanding — extrapolating backward gave the first observational evidence for the Big Bang
Earth sits at the center of the universe — since everything else is moving away from us specifically
Galaxies are stationary — the redshift Hubble measured was an artifact of his telescope's design flaws
The universe is shrinking — Hubble's data were misinterpreted for decades before being corrected later
questions.context: Hubble's measurements built on Vesto Slipher's earlier redshift observations and used Henrietta Leavitt's period-luminosity relation for Cepheid variable stars to gauge distances. The 'Hubble constant' (H₀ ~70 km/s/Mpc) measures the expansion rate. Georges Lemaître independently proposed the Big Bang in 1927. Modern measurements of H₀ via supernovae versus CMB show a tension (~9% disagreement) that remains an active research topic.

questions.question: The 1998 supernova-survey teams led by Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt, and Adam Riess made a startling discovery that earned them the 2011 Nobel in Physics. What did they find?
questions.answer: The expansion of the universe is accelerating, not slowing as gravity alone would predict, driven by 'dark energy'
choices: The expansion of the universe is accelerating, not slowing as gravity alone would predict, driven by 'dark energy'
The expansion of the universe is exactly stable, gravity perfectly balances dark energy at all scales
The universe is contracting toward a Big Crunch within the next billion years according to their data
The universe is exactly the size predicted by Einstein in 1915, and has not changed in measurable ways
questions.context: Type Ia supernovae have nearly constant peak brightness, making them 'standard candles' for measuring cosmic distances. Both teams independently found distant supernovae were fainter than expected — meaning farther away — meaning the universe's expansion had been speeding up. About 68% of the universe's energy content is 'dark energy,' a label for whatever is driving acceleration. Its physical nature remains one of the biggest open mysteries in physics.

questions.question: The Apollo missions brought back about 382 kg of Moon rock. One of the biggest scientific findings from analyzing those samples was about the Moon's age and origin. What did the rocks reveal?
questions.answer: The Moon is about 4.5 billion years old — consistent with the giant-impact hypothesis of a Mars-sized body striking proto-Earth
choices: The Moon is about 4.5 billion years old — consistent with the giant-impact hypothesis of a Mars-sized body striking proto-Earth
The Moon is younger than Earth by 2 billion years — meaning it must have been captured from another solar system
The Moon is much older than Earth itself — meaning the Earth-Moon system is two unrelated objects in space
The Moon's rocks were chemically identical to space debris — confirming the Moon is a captured asteroid
questions.context: Apollo samples show ages between roughly 3.1 and 4.4 billion years for the highland anorthosites and mare basalts. Oxygen-isotope ratios match Earth's mantle very closely, supporting the giant-impact hypothesis: a Mars-sized body (Theia) struck the proto-Earth ~4.5 Gya, ejecting debris that coalesced into the Moon. This explains why the Moon is large relative to its parent planet (a rarity in the solar system) and why it has so little iron.

questions.question: Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh at Lowell Observatory in Arizona. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union demoted it from planet status to 'dwarf planet.' What was the specific reason for the reclassification?
questions.answer: Pluto hasn't cleared its orbital neighborhood of other bodies — Eris, Haumea, and many Kuiper Belt objects share its zone
choices: Pluto hasn't cleared its orbital neighborhood of other bodies — Eris, Haumea, and many Kuiper Belt objects share its zone
Pluto turned out not to exist — Tombaugh's discovery was retracted in 2006 after telescope errors were found
Pluto is too cold to be considered a planet — the IAU set a minimum-temperature requirement that excluded it
Pluto orbits the Sun in the wrong direction compared to other planets — making it disqualified from membership
questions.context: The IAU's 2006 definition requires a planet to (1) orbit the Sun, (2) be massive enough for hydrostatic equilibrium (roundness), and (3) have cleared its orbital neighborhood. Pluto fails the third criterion. Eris (discovered 2005, briefly thought to be larger than Pluto) was the trigger for the redefinition. New Horizons flew by Pluto in 2015, revealing nitrogen glaciers and a heart-shaped plain (Tombaugh Regio).

questions.question: The auroras — Northern Lights and Southern Lights — happen when charged particles from the Sun reach Earth's upper atmosphere. Why do the lights mostly appear near the poles, not the equator?
questions.answer: Earth's magnetic field funnels solar particles toward the poles, where they slam into atmospheric molecules and make them glow
choices: Earth's magnetic field funnels solar particles toward the poles, where they slam into atmospheric molecules and make them glow
The atmosphere is thinner at the poles so solar light shines through it more brightly than near the equator
Polar ice reflects the auroral glow upward, equatorial regions absorb it instead of showing it overhead
Solar particles are deflected only by daylight, and the polar regions get less sun during winter months
questions.context: Earth's magnetic field is roughly dipolar — field lines converge at the magnetic poles. Solar wind particles (mostly protons and electrons) spiral along field lines and dump energy into the upper atmosphere ~100-300 km up. Oxygen produces green and red colors; nitrogen produces blue and purple. Major solar storms can push the aurora as far south as the Caribbean — the 1859 Carrington Event was visible from Hawaii and Mexico.

questions.question: A solar flare in 1859 — the Carrington Event — caused telegraph stations to spark, electrocute operators, and even send signals with the batteries disconnected. What concerns modern scientists about a repeat?
questions.answer: Today's power grids and satellites would be far more vulnerable than 1859 telegraph wires were to similar geomagnetic damage
choices: Today's power grids and satellites would be far more vulnerable than 1859 telegraph wires were to similar geomagnetic damage
Today's atmosphere has thinned enough that another Carrington-level flare would set surface forests on fire globally
Today's compass equipment is no longer in use, so navigation would be unaffected by any future solar storm
Today's Sun is dimmer than in 1859, so a Carrington-magnitude event is now physically impossible to occur
questions.context: The Carrington Event was observed by amateur astronomer Richard Carrington on September 1, 1859 and triggered worldwide auroras and telegraph chaos. A 2012 coronal mass ejection of similar magnitude narrowly missed Earth — it crossed our orbit 9 days behind us. Modern grid operators have hardening plans, but global recovery from a direct Carrington-level hit would likely take many months and trillions of dollars.

questions.question: Nicolaus Copernicus wrote *De Revolutionibus* in the 1530s but didn't publish until 1543. According to legend, a printed copy was placed in his hands the day he died. What was the radical claim of the book?
questions.answer: The Sun, not the Earth, sits at the center of the planetary system, the Earth itself moves
choices: The Sun, not the Earth, sits at the center of the planetary system, the Earth itself moves
The Earth is flat, not round, the prevailing spherical-Earth view was wrong since classical times
The Moon is a giant mirror reflecting the cities of an inhabited continent on its other face
Stars are distant suns with planets, but the Earth still rests at the center of the cosmos overall
questions.context: Copernicus delayed publication for decades, partly out of caution. The opening dedication to Pope Paul III argued the heliocentric model wasn't a theological threat. The book's introduction (added by editor Andreas Osiander without Copernicus's authorization) tried to soften the claim as a 'mathematical hypothesis,' not physical truth. Galileo and Kepler later treated it as physical truth.

questions.question: Galileo Galilei was tried by the Roman Inquisition in 1633 for advocating heliocentrism after warnings to stop. What was his actual fate, and when did the Catholic Church formally close the case?
questions.answer: House arrest until his death in 1642, and the Vatican formally rehabilitated him only in 1992 under John Paul II
choices: House arrest until his death in 1642, and the Vatican formally rehabilitated him only in 1992 under John Paul II
Burned at the stake in 1633, the same year as his trial, after refusing to recant his views
Acquitted, and apologized to by the Pope immediately after a fair trial conducted with full evidence
Exiled to the New World where he founded the first scientific society in colonial Massachusetts
questions.context: Galileo recanted his heliocentric views under threat. He spent his last years at his villa in Arcetri near Florence, going blind but continuing scientific work (he published *Two New Sciences* in 1638). Pope John Paul II in 1992 accepted the report of a 13-year Vatican commission that found the 1633 judgment unjust, formally closing one of the most famous science-church controversies in history.

questions.question: Isaac Newton's *Principia Mathematica* (1687) was the result of less than two years of intense writing, but Newton had been thinking about gravity for decades. Why did he finally write it up?
questions.answer: Edmund Halley visited him, asked about planetary orbits, then funded the publication out of his own pocket
choices: Edmund Halley visited him, asked about planetary orbits, then funded the publication out of his own pocket
Robert Hooke threatened to publish first, Newton rushed to print to claim priority for the inverse-square law
The British Crown commissioned the work, and paid Newton handsomely for completing it within a deadline
Newton's bankruptcy forced him to sell the manuscript to a printer in order to pay off his creditors fully
questions.context: Edmund Halley (the comet) asked Newton in 1684 what curve a planet would follow under an inverse-square gravitational force. Newton replied 'an ellipse' — and then couldn't find the proof. He rederived it and over the next 18 months expanded the work into the *Principia*. The Royal Society's budget was exhausted on a fish book, so Halley funded the printing himself. Newton always remained suspicious that Hooke had also derived the inverse-square law independently.

questions.question: Charles Darwin returned from the Beagle voyage in 1836 with notebooks suggesting species change over time. He didn't publish *On the Origin of Species* until 1859. What pushed him to finally publish?
questions.answer: Alfred Russel Wallace mailed Darwin a manuscript proposing the same theory, Darwin rushed his own to press
choices: Alfred Russel Wallace mailed Darwin a manuscript proposing the same theory, Darwin rushed his own to press
Queen Victoria personally requested that Darwin publish his theory within the year for the British Empire's prestige
Darwin's wife refused to live with him until he published, under threat of formal religious separation
Darwin won a contest set by the Royal Society for the best theory of species change in the natural world
questions.context: Darwin received Wallace's letter from Indonesia in June 1858 containing essentially the same theory of natural selection. Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged a joint presentation at the Linnean Society on July 1, 1858. Darwin then wrote *Origin* in a year and published in November 1859. The 23-year delay had been driven partly by his caution about religious controversy and partly by his thoroughness in gathering supporting evidence.

questions.question: Gregor Mendel's pea-plant work, completed by 1863 and published 1866, established the foundations of genetics. What happened to his work between publication and his death in 1884?
questions.answer: It was almost completely ignored — Mendel died not knowing his work would later become the basis of modern genetics
choices: It was almost completely ignored — Mendel died not knowing his work would later become the basis of modern genetics
It was attacked as heretical by the Catholic Church — leading to his excommunication from the monastery
It became immediately famous worldwide — he was elected to the Royal Society and won numerous prizes
It was correctly recognized by Darwin himself — who incorporated Mendel's results into later editions of Origin
questions.context: Mendel sent his 1866 paper to Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli, a leading botanist, who failed to grasp its significance and discouraged Mendel from further work in that direction. Mendel became abbot of his monastery and ran out of time for research. His work was rediscovered around 1900 by Hugo de Vries (Netherlands), Carl Correns (Germany), and Erich von Tschermak (Austria) — each working independently, each finding the laws Mendel had already established 34 years earlier.

questions.question: Mendel's work was rediscovered around 1900 by three botanists working independently. Why did the timing matter — what had changed in the intervening decades to make scientists ready for it?
questions.answer: Chromosomes had been observed during cell division, giving scientists a physical structure that could carry Mendel's 'factors'
choices: Chromosomes had been observed during cell division, giving scientists a physical structure that could carry Mendel's 'factors'
Computers had been invented to handle the statistical analysis Mendel's data required for verification
DNA had been isolated and sequenced, making the connection to Mendel's inheritance patterns obvious
Eugenics laws in the United States required scientific justification for marriage restrictions, and sterilization
questions.context: Walther Flemming described chromosomes during mitosis in the 1880s. Theodor Boveri and Walter Sutton independently proposed in 1902-1903 that chromosomes carry Mendel's inheritance factors. Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit-fly work at Columbia (1910s) confirmed the chromosomal theory of inheritance. By the 1900s, scientists had a physical home for Mendel's abstract 'factors' — making his work suddenly look like the key to biology rather than a curiosity.

questions.question: James Watson and Francis Crick published their double-helix paper in *Nature* on April 25, 1953. A key piece of evidence was an X-ray diffraction image of DNA known as Photo 51. Who took it, and what role does she play in the story?
questions.answer: Rosalind Franklin produced it at King's College London — and her data were shown to Watson without her knowledge
choices: Rosalind Franklin produced it at King's College London — and her data were shown to Watson without her knowledge
Maurice Wilkins took it personally — Franklin had no role in the X-ray work at King's College that year
James Watson took it himself in his Cambridge lab — making Franklin's contribution exaggerated by later writers
It was taken by an unknown lab technician — its true origin has remained a mystery to historians ever since
questions.context: Photo 51 was taken by Raymond Gosling under Rosalind Franklin's supervision in May 1952. Maurice Wilkins (Franklin's colleague at King's, with whom she had a famously poor working relationship) showed the photograph to Watson without Franklin's knowledge or consent in early 1953. The image revealed the helical structure unambiguously. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958; the 1962 Nobel went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins (Nobels are not awarded posthumously).

questions.question: Marie Curie remained the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences for over a century. What were her two Nobels for?
questions.answer: Physics 1903 (with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) for radioactivity; Chemistry 1911 (alone) for polonium and radium
choices: Physics 1903 (with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) for radioactivity; Chemistry 1911 (alone) for polonium and radium
Medicine 1903 for X-ray therapy; Peace 1911 for her humanitarian work during World War I
Literature 1903 for her chemistry textbook; Physics 1911 for the discovery of neutrons
Physiology 1903 for radium therapy in cancer; Chemistry 1911 for periodic-table contributions
questions.context: Marie Curie (Maria Skłodowska, born 1867 in Warsaw) and Pierre Curie discovered polonium (named after her homeland) and radium in 1898. She invented the term 'radioactivity.' During WWI she organized mobile X-ray units ('petites Curies') for battlefield diagnosis. She died in 1934 from aplastic anemia, almost certainly from her decades of radiation exposure. Her notebooks remain so radioactive they are kept in lead-lined boxes.

questions.question: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren first proposed in 1982 that bacteria — not stress or spicy food — caused most stomach ulcers. Why did the medical establishment refuse to accept it?
questions.answer: It violated the long-standing belief that stomach acid kills bacteria — and questioned a profitable antacid industry
choices: It violated the long-standing belief that stomach acid kills bacteria — and questioned a profitable antacid industry
Marshall and Warren had no medical degrees — so their work was disqualified on credential grounds alone
Their experiments had been performed only on rats, not humans — and the journal refused publication
Their hypothesis was identical to a known fraud from the 1950s — making peer reviewers suspicious
questions.context: *Helicobacter pylori* lives in the stomach's mucous lining and is well-adapted to the acid environment. Pre-1982 ulcer treatment involved antacids and acid-suppressing drugs — a multi-billion-dollar market. Marshall struggled to find a journal that would publish his findings. After years of resistance, he drank a beaker of H. pylori himself in 1984, developed gastritis, then cured it with antibiotics. Marshall and Warren won the 2005 Nobel in Medicine.

questions.question: Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand-washing in maternity wards cut deaths from puerperal fever by ten-fold. What was the establishment response that ultimately drove him into an asylum?
questions.answer: His colleagues felt insulted by the suggestion that gentlemen-doctors carried death on their hands, and dismissed him
choices: His colleagues felt insulted by the suggestion that gentlemen-doctors carried death on their hands, and dismissed him
His colleagues immediately adopted hand-washing, but Semmelweis took offense at not being credited enough
His colleagues confirmed the result but said his proposed mechanism violated divine providence's will
His colleagues lost interest because the mortality numbers were considered insignificant overall
questions.context: Semmelweis worked at Vienna General Hospital. He noticed Ward 1 (run by doctors) had ~18% death rate, while Ward 2 (run by midwives) had ~2%. The doctors had been doing autopsies before delivering babies. After he required chlorinated-lime hand-washing, doctor-ward deaths dropped to match the midwife ward. The medical establishment rejected the finding because Semmelweis couldn't explain WHY (germ theory came later). He died in 1865, possibly from sepsis after being beaten by asylum guards.

questions.question: Joseph Lister extended Semmelweis's hand-washing insight to surgery in the 1860s, using carbolic acid sprays to reduce post-operative infection. What earlier scientist provided Lister with the theoretical foundation for why antisepsis works?
questions.answer: Louis Pasteur — whose germ-theory experiments showed microbes caused fermentation and disease
choices: Louis Pasteur — whose germ-theory experiments showed microbes caused fermentation and disease
Isaac Newton — whose gravity laws explained why heavy infection-causing fluids settled into wounds
