Robert Boyle — whose gas laws predicted that hot air alone could sterilize surgical instruments without chemicals
Antoine Lavoisier — whose chemistry of oxygen showed surgical wounds needed sealing off from air
questions.context: Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments (1860s) demonstrated that microorganisms in the air caused spoilage and disease — not 'spontaneous generation.' Lister extended the insight to surgery, sterilizing instruments and using carbolic-acid sprays during operations. Surgical mortality dropped dramatically. The Listerine mouthwash brand (1879) is named after him. Pasteur's later work on vaccines (rabies 1885) further established germ theory as the foundation of modern medicine.

questions.question: Stanley Prusiner won the 1997 Nobel for proposing in 1982 that mad-cow disease and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease are caused by misfolded proteins — 'prions' — with no DNA or RNA at all. Why was this controversial when proposed?
questions.answer: It seemed to violate biology's central dogma that all infectious agents must contain nucleic acids
choices: It seemed to violate biology's central dogma that all infectious agents must contain nucleic acids
It contradicted the laws of thermodynamics, proteins were not believed to fold spontaneously back then
It claimed cows had emotions like humans, which animal-rights critics seized on for political purposes
It was disproved within a year of publication, but Prusiner refused to retract his original paper
questions.context: The Central Dogma of molecular biology (Crick 1958) held that information flows DNA → RNA → protein. Prusiner's 'proteinaceous infectious particles' (prions) replicate by causing other normal proteins to misfold into the same disease-causing shape — passing on a structural pattern, not a genetic sequence. Many biologists rejected the idea for years. Prion diseases include scrapie in sheep, BSE (mad cow), CJD in humans, and chronic wasting disease in deer.

questions.question: Lynn Margulis proposed in 1967 that mitochondria — the energy-producing organelles in our cells — were originally free-living bacteria that became permanent residents inside larger cells. How was her idea received initially?
questions.answer: Mocked and rejected by mainstream biology for over a decade, until DNA evidence vindicated her by the 1980s
choices: Mocked and rejected by mainstream biology for over a decade, until DNA evidence vindicated her by the 1980s
Immediately celebrated, and adopted into all biology textbooks within the same year as publication
Banned by the American Society for Cell Biology, Margulis was barred from publishing for several decades
Confirmed by Margulis herself with a Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1968 the year after publication
questions.context: Margulis's 'serial endosymbiotic theory' faced fifteen rejections before publication in the *Journal of Theoretical Biology* (1967). She argued mitochondria (from oxygen-respiring bacteria) and chloroplasts (from cyanobacteria) had once been independent organisms. By the 1980s, DNA sequencing showed mitochondrial DNA resembles bacterial DNA more than the host cell's nuclear DNA — confirming her theory. She was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1983.

questions.question: Norman Borlaug's Green Revolution dwarf wheats transformed agriculture in Mexico, India, and Pakistan starting in the 1960s. Why specifically did he develop SHORT wheat varieties?
questions.answer: Short stalks could carry heavier grain heads without bending or breaking, preventing crop loss in storm winds
choices: Short stalks could carry heavier grain heads without bending or breaking, preventing crop loss in storm winds
Short stalks needed less fertilizer because they grew more slowly, and had a longer harvest season overall
Short stalks attracted fewer insects because pests preferred to lay eggs in tall plants with thicker stems
Short stalks gave a smaller harvest but could grow in deserts, solving food shortages in arid regions
questions.context: Traditional tall wheats grew long stalks that 'lodged' (fell over) when bearing heavy grain heads boosted by nitrogen fertilizer. Borlaug crossed Mexican wheats with Japanese Norin 10 dwarf varieties (developed by Orville Vogel). The semi-dwarf hybrids carried high grain yields without lodging. India's wheat harvest doubled in five years (1965-1970), preventing predicted famine. Borlaug won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize for his work.

questions.question: Tu Youyou won China's first Nobel in medicine (2015) for discovering artemisinin, the antimalarial drug now used worldwide. What was the unusual source of her insight?
questions.answer: A 4th-century Chinese herbal medicine text describing sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua) for fevers
choices: A 4th-century Chinese herbal medicine text describing sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua) for fevers
A Soviet biological-warfare textbook describing wormwood as a possible vector for spreading malaria
A NASA contract to investigate plants for use during the Mars-mission planning of the 1980s
Her own dream after a malaria fever, in which her grandmother told her exactly which plant to use
questions.context: Tu Youyou worked in Mao-era China under Project 523 to find a malaria treatment for Chinese troops in Vietnam. She and her team screened over 2,000 traditional remedies. The breakthrough came from Ge Hong's *Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies* (~340 AD), which described soaking sweet wormwood in cold water. That clue revealed that high heat destroyed the active compound — explaining why earlier extraction attempts had failed.

questions.question: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier shared the 2020 Nobel in Chemistry for CRISPR gene-editing. What was the original natural source of CRISPR — what's it for in nature?
questions.answer: A bacterial immune system that snips up the DNA of attacking viruses, repurposed by scientists into a precision-editing tool
choices: A bacterial immune system that snips up the DNA of attacking viruses, repurposed by scientists into a precision-editing tool
A toxin produced by jellyfish that scientists isolated, and converted into a glowing genetic marker
A failed cancer therapy from the 1990s that turned out to have unrelated DNA-editing capabilities
A natural DNA-repair mechanism in human eggs that was extracted, and applied to other species
questions.context: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats were observed in bacterial DNA in 1987 but their function wasn't understood for over twenty years. Jansen, Mojica, and others showed CRISPR + Cas proteins were a bacterial defense system: bacteria store viral DNA snippets, then use them as recognition templates to cut the same virus next time. Doudna and Charpentier's 2012 paper showed how to reprogram the system to cut any DNA sequence the scientist chooses — turning bacterial immunity into a gene-editing scalpel.

questions.question: CRISPR's first FDA-approved treatment was Casgevy in December 2023 for sickle cell disease. How does it actually treat patients?
questions.answer: Doctors take their bone-marrow cells — edit out the sickle gene with CRISPR in a dish, then reinfuse the corrected cells
choices: Doctors take their bone-marrow cells — edit out the sickle gene with CRISPR in a dish, then reinfuse the corrected cells
Doctors inject the CRISPR enzyme directly into the bloodstream — where it travels to bone marrow and edits DNA on contact
Doctors give the patient a daily pill containing CRISPR molecules — taken with water for several years to gradually fix the disease
Doctors do not need to do anything — CRISPR was repurposed as a vaccine and prevents sickle cell from developing in the first place
questions.context: Casgevy (exa-cel) edits the BCL11A gene to reactivate fetal hemoglobin, compensating for the sickle defect. Patients undergo a procedure similar to bone-marrow transplant: their hematopoietic stem cells are removed, edited ex vivo with CRISPR-Cas9, the patient is conditioned with chemotherapy to make room, and the edited cells are infused. Two early trial patients have remained free of vaso-occlusive crises for years. The approach also works for beta-thalassemia.

questions.question: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper won the 2024 Nobel in Chemistry alongside David Baker for AlphaFold — an AI system that solved a decades-old biology puzzle. What did AlphaFold actually solve?
questions.answer: Predicting the 3D folded shape of a protein from its amino-acid sequence, a problem unsolved for 50+ years
choices: Predicting the 3D folded shape of a protein from its amino-acid sequence, a problem unsolved for 50+ years
Predicting the next mass extinction event by simulating ecosystems across the entire planet at once
Inventing a new branch of mathematics for protein chemistry that was completely unrelated to AI methods
Curing all known forms of cancer by predicting which patients would respond to which treatments
questions.context: Protein folding — how a linear chain of amino acids folds into a specific 3D shape that determines function — had been a grand challenge in biochemistry since Christian Anfinsen's 1972 Nobel work showed sequence determines structure. The CASP competition (1994 onward) tracked progress. AlphaFold 2 (Hassabis, Jumper, DeepMind) achieved near-experimental accuracy in CASP14 (2020). AlphaFold's predicted structures for ~200 million proteins are now publicly available. David Baker (University of Washington) won the other half for designing entirely new proteins.

questions.question: Before AlphaFold, getting a protein's 3D structure required X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy — slow and expensive techniques. Why did this matter for medicine specifically?
questions.answer: Drug design depends on knowing how a target protein looks — AlphaFold dramatically accelerated this stage of research
choices: Drug design depends on knowing how a target protein looks — AlphaFold dramatically accelerated this stage of research
Doctors needed protein structures to diagnose patients — AlphaFold lets them skip the doctor visit entirely
Hospitals had to grow proteins in their labs — AlphaFold replaced this with computer models for direct treatment
Vaccines required individual structure determination for each patient — AlphaFold made personalized vaccines possible
questions.context: A typical drug molecule fits into a specific pocket on a target protein. Designing the drug requires knowing the protein's exact 3D shape — which used to require months of experimental work for a single protein. AlphaFold now predicts structures in minutes for any protein with a known sequence, dramatically reducing the early stages of drug discovery. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) is free and open. Structure-based drug design has become much more practical because of this.

questions.question: In 1907 Indiana passed the first compulsory sterilization law in world history, targeting people labeled 'feeble-minded' or 'unfit.' What name did the movement that pushed such laws across the US go by?
questions.answer: Eugenics — promoted as 'scientific' policy at major American universities and funded by Carnegie and Rockefeller
choices: Eugenics — promoted as 'scientific' policy at major American universities and funded by Carnegie and Rockefeller
Hygenics — a small fringe movement opposed by mainstream American medical authorities of the era
Eugnosticism — a religious revival movement that ended quickly once World War I broke out in Europe
Optomy — a public-health policy movement focused on vision care for poor American workers' children
questions.context: Eugenics had wide mainstream support in the early 20th century US — backed by Ivy League scientists, the American Medical Association, philanthropists Carnegie and Rockefeller, and progressive reformers. The Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor (Charles Davenport, Harry Laughlin) lobbied for sterilization laws nationwide. By the late 1920s, more than 20 US states had compulsory sterilization statutes on the books.

questions.question: In 1927 the US Supreme Court ruled 8-1 in *Buck v. Bell* that compulsory sterilization of Carrie Buck, a young Virginia woman labeled 'feeble-minded,' was constitutional. What infamous line did Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes write in the majority opinion?
questions.answer: 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough' — and the ruling has never been formally overturned
choices: 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough' — and the ruling has never been formally overturned
'Liberty requires careful breeding' — but Holmes recanted the opinion in his memoirs after retirement
'Science teaches us all we need to know' — a phrase Holmes later dropped from the official record
'The state has no role in family planning' — and the ruling was overturned within the same decade
questions.context: Carrie Buck's case was actually a test case orchestrated by sterilization advocates. Carrie's daughter Vivian was labeled 'imbecile' after a single brief exam at seven months old. Later scholarship has shown the IQ testing was rigged. Vivian made the honor roll in school before dying young. Carrie Buck herself was an ordinary woman — pregnant after being raped by a relative of her foster family. *Buck v. Bell* has never been formally overturned, though no state currently uses it for sterilization.

questions.question: California became the most aggressive American sterilization state under eugenics laws. How many Californians were sterilized under state law before the program tapered off?
questions.answer: More than 20,000 — most disproportionately poor, immigrant, or Spanish-speaking, well into the 1960s
choices: More than 20,000 — most disproportionately poor, immigrant, or Spanish-speaking, well into the 1960s
Around 50 — California's law was on the books but rarely enforced and considered symbolic
Around 100,000 — but mostly white middle-class Americans rather than minorities or immigrants
Zero — California passed the law but never implemented it because of immediate legal challenges
questions.context: California's 1909 sterilization law authorized state officials to sterilize people in mental institutions. Over 20,000 Californians were sterilized through 1979 — disproportionately Mexican-American, poor, and labeled 'mentally deficient.' Nazi eugenicists explicitly cited California's program as a model in the 1930s. California formally apologized in 2003. A 2021 California law authorized reparations for surviving victims of state-sanctioned sterilization.

questions.question: Margaret Sanger, founder of what would become Planned Parenthood, was a prominent eugenicist who wrote and spoke about race and reproductive policy in the 1910s-1930s. What's her own most direct statement people often point to?
questions.answer: Her writings called for limiting reproduction by people she described as 'human weeds', and 'morons'
choices: Her writings called for limiting reproduction by people she described as 'human weeds', and 'morons'
Her writings explicitly opposed eugenics, and were misquoted by Catholic critics of her clinics
Her writings never touched on race or class, focusing exclusively on women's individual rights
Her writings called for universal forced sterilization of all human beings without any exceptions
questions.context: Sanger's *The Pivot of Civilization* (1922) and her writings in *Birth Control Review* explicitly endorsed eugenic goals. She opened the first US birth-control clinic in Brooklyn (1916) and later founded what became Planned Parenthood. She lectured to the Ku Klux Klan in 1926. The 'Negro Project' (1939) was framed in her own letters as needing Black ministers to prevent the idea that 'we want to exterminate the Negro population.' Planned Parenthood removed her name from its New York City clinic in 2020.

questions.question: The Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor on Long Island was the operational center of American eugenics from 1910 to 1939. Who funded it, and who ran it?
questions.answer: Funded by Carnegie and Rockefeller — run by Charles Davenport and Harry Laughlin, who lobbied for sterilization laws
choices: Funded by Carnegie and Rockefeller — run by Charles Davenport and Harry Laughlin, who lobbied for sterilization laws
Funded by the US Department of Agriculture — and run as a routine cattle-breeding research station only
Funded by private donations from concerned families — and run by religious leaders rather than scientists
Funded by the Soviet government — as a project to spread Marxist racial theory in the United States
questions.context: Charles Davenport founded the Eugenics Record Office in 1910 with Carnegie Institution money. Harry Laughlin, his deputy, drafted the Model Eugenical Sterilization Law (1922) that influenced US state laws. The ERO collected pedigree data on hundreds of thousands of Americans, classifying families by traits like 'shiftlessness' and 'feeble-mindedness.' Laughlin received an honorary degree from the University of Heidelberg in 1936 for his eugenics work. Carnegie withdrew funding in 1939 as the methodology was discredited.

questions.question: Madison Grant's 1916 book *The Passing of the Great Race* was a popular American eugenics text. According to Adolf Hitler's own statement, what was the book to him?
questions.answer: 'My bible,' as Hitler reportedly told Grant in a letter — and Nazi T4 explicitly modeled American sterilization precedent
choices: 'My bible,' as Hitler reportedly told Grant in a letter — and Nazi T4 explicitly modeled American sterilization precedent
A book he had never heard of — Hitler had no awareness of any American eugenicist authors before the war
A book he publicly denounced — Hitler said American eugenics was 'too soft' and inferior to German thinking
A book he banned in Nazi Germany — Hitler considered Grant's racial categories scientifically wrong
questions.context: Hitler wrote Grant in the 1920s expressing admiration for *The Passing of the Great Race*. Grant was a prominent New York lawyer, conservationist, and self-trained anthropologist. He also helped draft the 1924 US Immigration Act's national-origin quotas. The Nazi T4 program (1939-1941) explicitly cited American eugenic sterilization as a model, and Nazi defense lawyers at Nuremberg pointed to *Buck v. Bell* as an American precedent for state-mandated reproductive policy.

questions.question: The Nuremberg Code (1947) was written by judges in the trial of Nazi doctors after World War II. What's its first and most famous principle?
questions.answer: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential to medical experimentation
choices: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential to medical experimentation
Medical doctors should be paid the highest salaries possible to attract talent worldwide
Patients have the right to immediate access to all of their medical records on request
Doctors must take an oath of secrecy to protect future patients' privacy in courts of law
questions.context: The Nuremberg Doctors' Trial (1946-1947) prosecuted 23 Nazi physicians and administrators for human experimentation in concentration camps. The 10-point Nuremberg Code articulated standards for ethical medical research, with voluntary informed consent as the foundational principle. The Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964) and the Belmont Report (US, 1979) built on Nuremberg. The Code remains the ethical foundation for modern research ethics, including IRB oversight and informed-consent requirements.

questions.question: The Tuskegee Syphilis Study ran from 1932 to 1972 — 40 years of US Public Health Service research on Black sharecroppers in Alabama. What did the men consent to, and what was actually done?
questions.answer: They were told they were being treated for 'bad blood' — but they were studied untreated even after penicillin became available
choices: They were told they were being treated for 'bad blood' — but they were studied untreated even after penicillin became available
They consented to a vaccine trial — and received the vaccine on schedule with no problems whatsoever
They consented to syphilis research and were paid generously — receiving the most modern available treatment
They were soldiers volunteering for war-related medical research — receiving full informed consent forms
questions.context: The US Public Health Service enrolled 600 Black men (399 with syphilis, 201 without) at the Tuskegee Institute in 1932. The men were told they were being treated for 'bad blood' but received no treatment — even after penicillin became standard care in 1947. The study was exposed by Associated Press reporter Jean Heller in 1972. It ended that year. Final settlement reached survivors and their families. President Clinton formally apologized in 1997. The case became a foundational example in modern bioethics and informed consent.

questions.question: Henrietta Lacks died of cervical cancer in 1951 at Johns Hopkins. Her tumor cells, taken without her knowledge, became 'HeLa' — the first immortal human cell line. What's the lasting ethics question her case raises?
questions.answer: Patients have rights over their biological samples — but Lacks's family received nothing for decades while industry profited
choices: Patients have rights over their biological samples — but Lacks's family received nothing for decades while industry profited
Patients have no rights to their tissue samples — the medical establishment confirmed this in court repeatedly
Patients receive automatic royalties from cell-line research — Lacks's family was paid yearly from 1951 onward
Patients can sue freely over cell-line use — the legal foundation has been clear since the 1950s in US courts
questions.context: HeLa cells have been used in over 70,000 medical research papers and many billions of dollars in industry. Rebecca Skloot's *The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks* (2010) brought the story to wide public attention. NIH reached an agreement with the Lacks family in 2013 about HeLa genome data access. The case spurred ongoing discussion of biospecimen rights, informed consent, and benefit-sharing — particularly when the original patient was Black and poor.

questions.question: Modern hospitals require 'informed consent' forms for procedures and research. What earlier 20th-century event most directly drove this legal and ethical requirement into US medical practice?
questions.answer: The Nuremberg Code (1947) after the Nazi doctors' trial — built on by Belmont (1979) and federal regulations
choices: The Nuremberg Code (1947) after the Nazi doctors' trial — built on by Belmont (1979) and federal regulations
The Hippocratic Oath (~400 BC) — which was directly incorporated into US federal law in the 1920s
The American Medical Association's founding (1847) — which made informed consent mandatory from the start
The Vietnam War (1960s-1970s) — when veterans demanded consent reform in returning-soldier medical care
questions.context: Pre-Nuremberg, informed consent was an aspiration but not legally enforced in the US. The Nuremberg Code established it as foundational. The 1964 Declaration of Helsinki refined it. The 1974 National Research Act (after Tuskegee was exposed) created the National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects. The Belmont Report (1979) articulated principles (respect, beneficence, justice). 45 CFR 46 (the 'Common Rule') codified IRB review and informed consent for federally funded research.

questions.question: A 'replication crisis' was named after researchers tried to redo many published studies and found most could not be repeated. What's the recognition skill for a teenager reading 'NEW STUDY SHOWS X' headlines?
questions.answer: Wait for replication — a single finding is weak evidence, no matter the journal or how confident the headline sounds
choices: Wait for replication — a single finding is weak evidence, no matter the journal or how confident the headline sounds
Trust every study from prestigious journals — peer review eliminates errors before publication, full stop
Reject all scientific research as fake — treat science headlines the same as gossip about random celebrities
Believe the most recent study above any earlier work — newer research always overrides older established work
questions.context: The 'replication crisis' was anchored by John Ioannidis's 2005 paper 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False,' the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 attempt to replicate 100 psychology studies (only ~36% replicated), and dramatic individual cases like Stapel (50+ retractions, 2011). Pre-registration of hypotheses, larger sample sizes, open data, and registered reports are tools the field has adopted in response. The kid's skill is intermediate: not 'trust everything,' not 'reject everything,' but 'wait for the second study.'

questions.question: Diederik Stapel was a star Dutch social psychologist at Tilburg University whose work appeared in *Science* and major journals. In 2011 his career imploded. What happened?
questions.answer: He confessed to fabricating data in dozens of papers — over 50 of his published works were eventually retracted
choices: He confessed to fabricating data in dozens of papers — over 50 of his published works were eventually retracted
He was caught accepting bribes from corporate sponsors — but his actual data was sound on inspection
He plagiarized other authors' work — but his original conclusions remained intact and respected in the field
He was wrongly accused but cleared after extensive investigation — and his career fully recovered
questions.context: Three of Stapel's junior researchers reported irregularities in 2011. An investigation led by Willem Levelt found he had been fabricating data for years — sometimes just making up numbers in his hotel room before showing them to graduate students. Over 50 of his papers were retracted by 2024. The case became a foundational example of how prestigious credentials, top-journal placement, and peer review can fail to catch outright fabrication. His memoir *Faking Science* (2014) is a chilling firsthand account.

questions.question: The Open Science Collaboration's 'Reproducibility Project: Psychology' was published in *Science* in 2015. What did it find when researchers tried to replicate 100 published psychology studies?
questions.answer: Only about 36% replicated with statistical significance — and effect sizes were typically half the original published values
choices: Only about 36% replicated with statistical significance — and effect sizes were typically half the original published values
Around 95% replicated cleanly — psychology was confirmed as one of the more rigorous social sciences
All 100 studies replicated exactly — the project was used to defend the discipline against critics
None of the studies could be replicated at all — the entire psychology literature was discarded
questions.context: The Reproducibility Project Psychology recruited 270 contributing scientists and tried to replicate 100 studies published in three leading psychology journals (2008). Of the 97 with positive results in the original paper, only 35 (36%) yielded statistically significant replications. Mean effect sizes were about half. The project triggered serious methodological reform in psychology — pre-registration, larger samples, open data — though similar problems exist in biomedical, economic, and machine-learning research.

questions.question: Brian Wansink at Cornell ran the popular Food and Brand Lab, producing widely-cited findings on portion control and bottomless soup bowls. What happened to his work between 2016 and 2018?
questions.answer: Critics found dozens of statistical inconsistencies — Wansink lost his Cornell position and had 18+ papers retracted
choices: Critics found dozens of statistical inconsistencies — Wansink lost his Cornell position and had 18+ papers retracted
His work was confirmed by independent replication — and he was given a Nobel Prize for nutrition science
He was promoted to Cornell's presidency — and his work became required reading in public-health programs
He retired voluntarily — and his findings remained the consensus on portion-size and eating behavior
questions.context: A 2016 blog post by Wansink encouraging junior researchers to 'reslice' data for publishable patterns triggered scrutiny. Independent statisticians like Tim van der Zee found numerical inconsistencies across many of his published papers. Cornell investigated and concluded in 2018 that Wansink had committed academic misconduct. He resigned. At least 18 papers were formally retracted. His bottomless-soup-bowl study and other findings — long cited in policy debates — were discredited.

questions.question: The Surgisphere scandal of 2020 was one of the fastest implosions in modern medical research. What was published, where, and how quickly was it retracted?
questions.answer: Two papers in *The Lancet* and *NEJM* on COVID-19 treatments — retracted within weeks once the data couldn't be produced
choices: Two papers in *The Lancet* and *NEJM* on COVID-19 treatments — retracted within weeks once the data couldn't be produced
A single paper in *Nature* on COVID origins — confirmed independently and never retracted at any point
A textbook on emergency medicine — and the publisher refused to retract despite multiple complaints
A bioterrorism warning by the CDC — and the report was quietly removed without explanation
questions.context: Surgisphere Corporation claimed to operate a massive multinational hospital database. The May 2020 *Lancet* paper used it to claim hydroxychloroquine increased COVID mortality; the *NEJM* paper looked at blood-pressure medications. WHO suspended HCQ trials based on the *Lancet* findings. Within weeks, requests for data verification revealed the dataset's authenticity couldn't be confirmed. Both papers were retracted in June 2020. The episode shows how a single fabricated paper can affect policy in real time — and how the system can correct fast when scrutinized.

questions.question: In October 2020 three epidemiologists from Stanford, Harvard, and Oxford published the Great Barrington Declaration. What did it actually propose?
questions.answer: 'Focused protection' of vulnerable people while letting younger — and healthier populations resume normal life
choices: 'Focused protection' of vulnerable people while letting younger — and healthier populations resume normal life
Universal lockdowns extended for at least three more years — across the entire global population
Mandatory vaccination of all citizens including infants — backed by enforcement of fines and arrests
Closing schools permanently — replacing them with online-only learning into the next decade
questions.context: Jay Bhattacharya (Stanford epidemiologist, MD/PhD), Martin Kulldorff (Harvard biostatistician), and Sunetra Gupta (Oxford epidemiologist) wrote the Declaration at the American Institute for Economic Research. It argued lockdowns caused unequal harm — protecting older laptop-class workers while displacing harm onto younger working-class and Third World populations — and recommended targeting protection to the elderly while letting natural immunity develop in lower-risk groups. Over 60,000 doctors and scientists signed.

questions.question: How did NIH director Francis Collins respond to the Great Barrington Declaration in October 2020, according to FOIA'd emails released later?
questions.answer: He privately emailed Anthony Fauci calling for 'a quick, and devastating takedown' of the Declaration's authors
choices: He privately emailed Anthony Fauci calling for 'a quick, and devastating takedown' of the Declaration's authors
He praised the Declaration in a public statement, and invited the authors to NIH for policy discussions
He ignored the Declaration completely, and the FOIA emails confirmed he had never heard of it
He commissioned a peer-review panel to evaluate the Declaration's claims with full scientific rigor
questions.context: House Judiciary Committee subpoenas in 2023 released Collins's October 8, 2020 email to Fauci about 'a quick and devastating takedown.' Collins called the GBD signatories 'three fringe epidemiologists' despite their Stanford, Harvard, and Oxford affiliations. In March 2025, the Trump administration nominated Bhattacharya as NIH director — the same agency Collins had run. Bhattacharya was confirmed and serves as the 18th NIH director. The arc from 'fringe' label to NIH directorship within five years is one of the more visible reversals in modern US science policy.

questions.question: Jay Bhattacharya is now the 18th Director of the National Institutes of Health, confirmed in March 2025. What's his academic background, prior to becoming a national figure during COVID?
questions.answer: Stanford School of Medicine professor (MD and Stanford economics PhD), health policy researcher with hundreds of papers
choices: Stanford School of Medicine professor (MD and Stanford economics PhD), health policy researcher with hundreds of papers
Television host with no medical credentials, promoted to NIH after a popular daytime program
Pharmaceutical executive who came directly from a major drug company to lead the agency
Twitter influencer with a chemistry undergraduate degree but no formal medical training
questions.context: Bhattacharya holds MD and PhD degrees from Stanford. He's published hundreds of peer-reviewed papers on health policy, public health, and economics, with a particular focus on populations affected by health-care policy. The Great Barrington Declaration framed his public reputation during COVID. President Trump nominated him for NIH director in December 2024; the Senate confirmed him in March 2025. His nomination was controversial — Senator Bernie Sanders called him 'totally unfit'; supporters cited his return to mainstream public-health norms.

questions.question: Martin Kulldorff was a Harvard biostatistician serving on multiple federal vaccine advisory committees before he co-authored the Great Barrington Declaration in October 2020. What happened to his federal appointments afterward?
questions.answer: He was removed from the CDC's vaccine working group, and Harvard eventually let his contract expire in 2021
choices: He was removed from the CDC's vaccine working group, and Harvard eventually let his contract expire in 2021
He was promoted to lead the CDC's vaccine division, Harvard kept his position with full tenure
He resigned voluntarily and quietly, with no public controversy about his work during COVID
He remained on all advisory boards with no professional impact whatsoever from the Declaration
questions.context: Kulldorff invented the spatial scan statistic — the standard method for detecting disease outbreak clusters and used worldwide in public-health surveillance. He served on the CDC's Vaccine Safety Subgroup and an FDA advisory committee. After he co-authored the GBD and questioned aspects of COVID vaccine mandates, he was removed from CDC and FDA roles. Harvard later let his contract expire. He works now at the Brownstone Institute and Hillsdale College. His record on vaccine safety methodology is widely cited even by his critics.

questions.question: Steven Koonin was Undersecretary for Science under President Obama at the Department of Energy. In 2021 he published *Unsettled*. What was his central claim about climate science?
questions.answer: The IPCC's actual technical chapters don't support the catastrophist framing media coverage built on top of them
choices: The IPCC's actual technical chapters don't support the catastrophist framing media coverage built on top of them
Climate change is entirely fake, and all greenhouse-effect physics published since 1859 must be retracted
Climate change is much worse than the IPCC reports say, the catastrophist framing actually understates the risk
Climate change models are correct but should not be discussed in public policy or media coverage
questions.context: Koonin had a long career at Caltech and BP before serving in the Obama administration. *Unsettled* argues that the basic greenhouse physics is firm (Tyndall, Arrhenius), but climate sensitivity, attribution to humans for specific extreme events, and confidence in long-range predictions are far less certain than media coverage suggests. The book documents specific failed predictions, IPCC chapter quotes that differ from the Summary for Policymakers framing, and the cost-benefit analysis of mitigation versus adaptation. Koonin is not a 'denier'; he is the mature dissenting view.

questions.question: In 2007 Al Gore predicted Arctic sea ice would be 'completely gone' within 5-7 years. In 2008 the BBC reported NSIDC scientists predicting an ice-free summer Arctic by 2013. What actually happened by 2013?
questions.answer: Arctic September ice extent was about 5 million square km — well below recent averages but not zero, not even close to it
choices: Arctic September ice extent was about 5 million square km — well below recent averages but not zero, not even close to it
Arctic sea ice grew back to its 1980 levels — proving the original 2007 prediction had been deeply wrong
Arctic sea ice was exactly as Al Gore predicted — and the news was quietly downplayed by mainstream media
Arctic sea ice has never been measured — making any prediction about it scientifically meaningless overall
questions.context: Arctic September ice extent (the minimum each year) dropped substantially from the 1980s to roughly 2012, when a record low ~3.4 million km² was hit. It has since fluctuated between roughly 3.7 and 5 million km² in recent years — well above zero, well above an 'ice-free' summer. Multiple high-profile predictions of imminent ice-free Arctic summers (2007, 2008, 2014, 2018) have failed. Koonin's *Unsettled* discusses this case at length.

questions.question: Climate-policy discussions often cite the famous '97% of scientists agree' figure. Where did this number actually come from?
questions.answer: A 2013 paper by John Cook surveying abstracts — about a third took an explicit position, of which 97% endorsed warming
choices: A 2013 paper by John Cook surveying abstracts — about a third took an explicit position, of which 97% endorsed warming
A formal census of every climate scientist on the planet — confirmed by the IPCC peer-review process
A poll of US weather forecasters — and the actual figure was a 97% agreement on temperature trends
Direct measurement of consensus by AI-driven analysis of millions of papers — done in 2010 at MIT
questions.context: Cook et al. (2013) reviewed about 12,000 climate-related abstracts. Most either took no position or were neutral; of the roughly 4,000 that explicitly addressed human-caused warming, ~97% endorsed it. The '97% of scientists' formulation often misrepresents this: it's not about the magnitude of warming, climate sensitivity, attribution of extreme weather, or policy. The underlying figure also varies depending on what question is asked. The 97% framing was politically powerful but the underlying meaning was narrow.

questions.question: The Medieval Warm Period (MWP, ~950-1250) and Little Ice Age (LIA, ~1300-1850) appeared less prominently in the IPCC's famous 1998 'hockey stick' graph by Michael Mann. What's the criticism of that earlier graph?
questions.answer: It minimized natural climate variability before 1900 — making 20th-century warming appear unprecedented in 1000 years
choices: It minimized natural climate variability before 1900 — making 20th-century warming appear unprecedented in 1000 years
It overstated natural climate variability before 1900 — making 20th-century warming appear normal in 1000 years
It included only Australian tree-ring data — and was therefore not representative of the Northern Hemisphere
It was withdrawn by Mann himself in 1999 — and has never been used in any IPCC report since publication
questions.context: Michael Mann's 1998-1999 reconstructions showed Northern Hemisphere temperatures relatively flat through the past millennium then rising sharply in the 20th century — the 'hockey stick.' Critics including Steve McIntyre and Ross McKitrick argued the principal-components analysis and the choice of tree-ring proxies suppressed earlier warm intervals. Subsequent reconstructions (PAGES 2k Consortium, others) show more pre-industrial variability, including a clearer Medieval Warm Period and Little Ice Age. The basic finding that recent warming is significant is not in dispute; the historical comparison is.

questions.question: The 'Proximal Origin' paper (Andersen et al., *Nature Medicine*, March 2020) declared SARS-CoV-2 origin almost certainly natural. What did FOIA'd Slack messages from the authors reveal later about their actual views?
questions.answer: They privately suspected lab leak was plausible even while publicly declaring it almost certainly natural
choices: They privately suspected lab leak was plausible even while publicly declaring it almost certainly natural
They privately suspected the virus was bio-engineered as a weapon, but censored themselves for political reasons
Their private messages were never released, and the Proximal Origin paper has been fully confirmed by them
Their messages confirmed full agreement on natural origin, making the paper a model of scientific honesty
questions.context: Kristian Andersen, Eddie Holmes, Robert Garry, and the other authors had Slack messages and emails subpoenaed in 2023 by the House Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic. The released messages showed authors discussing the lab-leak hypothesis as plausible during the same period they were drafting the paper that dismissed it. Anthony Fauci and Jeremy Farrar had teleconferenced with the authors February 1, 2020 just before the paper was conceived. The paper was widely cited for over two years to label lab-leak claims 'misinformation.'

questions.question: By 2023, several US intelligence agencies — including FBI and Department of Energy — had publicly assessed that COVID-19 most likely came from a laboratory in Wuhan. What's the broader epistemic lesson from the lab-leak case?
questions.answer: A hypothesis labeled 'misinformation' in 2020 became respectable mainstream by 2023, labels can lag evidence by years
choices: A hypothesis labeled 'misinformation' in 2020 became respectable mainstream by 2023, labels can lag evidence by years
Intelligence agencies are never qualified to assess scientific questions, and their conclusions should be ignored
Lab leak has been definitively disproved by every later independent assessment of available evidence
Social media platforms always correctly flagged misinformation, and the platforms still stand by their decisions
questions.context: The FBI's 'moderate confidence' assessment of lab leak became public in February 2023. The Department of Energy reached a similar 'low confidence' conclusion. The CIA and other agencies remain split or undecided. The recognition: in early 2020, social-media platforms suppressed lab-leak discussion as 'misinformation,' often citing Proximal Origin. By 2023 the same hypothesis was the lead working theory in multiple US agencies. The episode is studied as a case of premature epistemic closure under political pressure.

questions.question: The Cochrane Collaboration's 2023 review of mask studies — led by Tom Jefferson — looked at the highest-quality randomized controlled trials. What was its conclusion about community masking against respiratory viruses?
questions.answer: Wearing masks in the community probably makes little to no difference to spread of influenza-like illness or COVID-19
choices: Wearing masks in the community probably makes little to no difference to spread of influenza-like illness or COVID-19
Wearing masks consistently reduces transmission by at least 80% under all real-world conditions
Wearing masks doubles the risk of infection, the review recommended banning them entirely
No reliable evidence exists on masking, the review demanded all studies on the topic be redone
questions.context: The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews ('Physical interventions to interrupt or reduce the spread of respiratory viruses,' Jefferson et al., January 30, 2023) was the most rigorous meta-analysis available, focusing on RCTs. Cochrane's editor-in-chief Karla Soares-Weiser later issued a statement claiming the abstract had been misinterpreted — Jefferson and other authors pushed back publicly. The original review remained available and its core finding (low evidence of efficacy for community masking) stood. The episode highlighted tension between RCT evidence and observational policy claims.

questions.question: Lockdowns were widely implemented in early 2020 as a COVID response. What did the 2022 Hanke-Herby-Jonung meta-analysis from Johns Hopkins find about their measured effectiveness?
questions.answer: Lockdowns reduced COVID-19 mortality in Europe, and the US by only about 0.2% on average
choices: Lockdowns reduced COVID-19 mortality in Europe, and the US by only about 0.2% on average
Lockdowns reduced COVID-19 mortality by exactly 95% across all countries that implemented them
Lockdowns increased COVID-19 mortality by about 50%, the policy made the pandemic worse
Lockdowns had no measurable effect, but they were widely judged necessary on policy grounds
questions.context: The Hanke-Herby-Jonung meta-analysis (2022, Johns Hopkins Institute for Applied Economics) reviewed studies on lockdown effectiveness and concluded the mortality benefit was very small while economic and social costs were enormous. The paper has been criticized methodologically and praised depending on the reviewer's prior. Other analyses found mixed effects. The broader recognition that emerged across many studies: 'lockdowns saved millions of lives' as a confident headline-level claim is no longer well-supported by the evidence as it has accumulated.

questions.question: School closures during 2020-2021 were a major component of the pandemic response. What does the bulk of subsequent evidence show about their effects on children?
questions.answer: Substantial learning loss, mental-health harm, and developmental setbacks, with lasting effects worst for poor and minority children
choices: Substantial learning loss, mental-health harm, and developmental setbacks, with lasting effects worst for poor and minority children
Substantial learning gains because children received more individualized parental attention at home
No effect at all, children fully recovered within weeks once schools eventually reopened nationwide
Improvement in standardized test scores, confirming online learning is superior to traditional schooling
questions.context: The 2022 NAEP ('Nation's Report Card') showed the largest declines in reading and math scores in the assessment's history. Studies from Stanford's CREDO, Harvard's Strategic Data Project, and McKinsey documented major learning losses concentrated in poorer and minority districts where school closures lasted longest. Sweden, which kept lower-grade schools open, showed smaller losses. The Great Barrington Declaration had warned of these effects in October 2020.

questions.question: Congress passed the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act in 1986, creating the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program. What did the act actually do in terms of legal liability for vaccine manufacturers?
questions.answer: It shielded manufacturers from most lawsuits over childhood vaccine injuries — routing claims through a federal claims court
choices: It shielded manufacturers from most lawsuits over childhood vaccine injuries — routing claims through a federal claims court
It made vaccine manufacturers fully liable in every state — creating new opportunities for class-action lawsuits
It declared vaccines exempt from all medical-ethics review — Congress removed every oversight requirement
It made vaccines free for all American children — and increased manufacturer profits to compensate
questions.context: Before 1986, multiple vaccine-injury lawsuits threatened US manufacturer participation in the childhood vaccine market. The NCVIA shielded manufacturers from most product-liability claims and created VICP as a no-fault compensation program. Critics including Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and attorney Aaron Siri argue the liability shield combined with mandate pressure removes the normal market discipline of liability litigation. Supporters argue it kept vaccines available. Both descriptions are accurate.

questions.question: The CDC's published childhood immunization schedule has expanded substantially since 1986. About how many doses were on the schedule by age 6 in 1986, versus by age 18 today?
questions.answer: About 11 doses by age 6 in 1986 — versus around 70+ doses by age 18 today, depending on the year and state
choices: About 11 doses by age 6 in 1986 — versus around 70+ doses by age 18 today, depending on the year and state
About 70 doses by age 6 in 1986 — and the schedule has slightly decreased since then to 50 doses
About 11 doses both in 1986 and today — the schedule has not changed at all in nearly four decades
About 5 doses in 1986 — and about 8 doses today, a small increase consistent with new disease threats
questions.context: The childhood vaccine schedule has grown with new vaccines for hepatitis B (1991), Hib, varicella (chickenpox, 1995), rotavirus, pneumococcal, hepatitis A, HPV, and meningococcal. Counting individual doses across the full age-18 schedule reaches roughly 70+ depending on what's included. The 1986 schedule covered fewer diseases with fewer doses. No published RCT has tested the combined schedule against any alternative; critics including Bhattacharya, Kulldorff, and Kennedy argue this is a gap in the evidence base for current US policy.

questions.question: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 — the only infectious human disease ever eradicated. Who was the last person to catch it naturally?
questions.answer: Ali Maow Maalin, a Somali hospital cook, caught smallpox in October 1977 and survived after treatment
choices: Ali Maow Maalin, a Somali hospital cook, caught smallpox in October 1977 and survived after treatment
An unknown Mongolian shepherd in the late 1980s caught smallpox from a smuggled live virus sample
A Soviet biological-warfare technician contracted it from a lab accident in 1979, and died from the disease
The last natural case was in 1812 in Ireland, the disease had been confined to laboratories thereafter
questions.context: The WHO Intensified Smallpox Eradication Program (1967-1980) used a ring-vaccination strategy targeting outbreaks rather than mass immunization. D.A. Henderson led the effort. The last natural case (variola minor) was Ali Maow Maalin in Somalia, October 1977. The last fatal case was Janet Parker, a British medical photographer who caught smallpox in 1978 from a Birmingham laboratory accident — the very last smallpox death in human history. WHO formally declared eradication May 8, 1980.

questions.question: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was announced safe and effective on April 12, 1955 — ten years to the day after Franklin Roosevelt died of polio. What's striking about Salk's choice not to patent it?
questions.answer: He declined to patent — telling Edward R. Murrow 'there is no patent. Could you patent the sun?'
choices: He declined to patent — telling Edward R. Murrow 'there is no patent. Could you patent the sun?'
He sold the patent for one dollar to the US government — keeping fully half of all future royalties
He patented it personally — and his estate continues to receive royalties from polio vaccine sales today
He licensed it exclusively to a single pharmaceutical company — granting them a permanent monopoly worldwide
questions.context: The Salk inactivated polio vaccine was developed at the University of Pittsburgh with funding from the March of Dimes. The 1954 Francis trial enrolled 1.8 million American children — the largest medical experiment in history. Salk's decision not to patent meant the vaccine was rapidly produced by multiple manufacturers and widely available. Albert Sabin's oral live-attenuated polio vaccine (1961) is what eventually drove polio toward worldwide eradication. As of 2025, wild polio remains in only a few areas of Afghanistan and Pakistan.

questions.question: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 but couldn't isolate the active compound at scale. Who actually did the chemistry that turned penicillin into a usable medicine in time for D-Day 1944?
questions.answer: Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, and Norman Heatley at Oxford, Florey and Chain shared Fleming's 1945 Nobel
choices: Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, and Norman Heatley at Oxford, Florey and Chain shared Fleming's 1945 Nobel
The German pharmaceutical company Bayer, they had completed all the work secretly by 1939 in Berlin
Fleming himself, by 1942 he had perfected penicillin production in his original London lab
An anonymous American GI medic who had bought penicillin tablets from a London pharmacy
questions.context: Florey, Chain, and Heatley at Oxford reactivated penicillin research in 1939. The first patient was treated in February 1941 — Albert Alexander, who improved dramatically but died when the limited supply ran out. American pharmaceutical companies (Pfizer, Merck) scaled up production using deep-tank fermentation. By D-Day 1944 mass-produced penicillin was saving Allied soldiers' lives. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel; Heatley's critical role in scaling was recognized only later, with an honorary Oxford doctorate in 1990.

questions.question: Penicillin transformed medicine but resistance was anticipated almost immediately. Who first warned about antibiotic resistance, and when?
questions.answer: Alexander Fleming himself — in his 1945 Nobel lecture, warning that misuse would breed resistant bacteria
choices: Alexander Fleming himself — in his 1945 Nobel lecture, warning that misuse would breed resistant bacteria
A pharmaceutical company in 1995 — making the warning a recent development of the late 20th century
The World Health Organization in 2015 — and there had been no earlier scientific awareness of resistance
It has never been an issue — penicillin remains as effective in 2026 as it was in the 1940s and 50s
questions.context: Fleming's 1945 Nobel Prize lecture warned: 'The time may come when penicillin can be bought by anyone in the shops. Then there is the danger that the ignorant man may easily underdose himself and by exposing his microbes to non-lethal quantities of the drug make them resistant.' Resistance emerged in *Staphylococcus aureus* within years. Modern multi-drug-resistant organisms (MRSA, CRE, XDR-TB) are a major public-health challenge. Antibiotic resistance is one area where scientific consensus has held firm from the beginning — and where the warnings have been borne out by experience.

questions.question: Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments in the 1860s definitively ended the idea of 'spontaneous generation' — the belief that maggots arose spontaneously from rotten meat. How did the elegant experimental design work?
questions.answer: Boiled broth in a flask with a long S-curved neck stayed sterile — microbes settled in the curve and never reached the broth
choices: Boiled broth in a flask with a long S-curved neck stayed sterile — microbes settled in the curve and never reached the broth
Sealed glass flasks always grew microbes — proving that life arose spontaneously from non-living matter alone
Microscopes showed microbes growing from rotten meat directly — confirming spontaneous generation as factual
Pasteur could not prove the experiment — and the question of spontaneous generation was never resolved
questions.context: Spontaneous generation (the idea that living things arise spontaneously from non-living matter) had been a serious scientific theory since Aristotle. Pasteur's 1860 experiment used flasks with long curved necks: the broth was boiled (sterilizing it), the necks let air in (so it wasn't simply 'lack of air'), but dust and microbes settled in the curve. The broth stayed sterile. Tip the flask so the broth touched the curve — and it spoiled within days. The experiment was decisive.

questions.question: Albert Einstein's 1905 'miracle year' produced four papers that transformed physics. What was the third paper — the one most directly relevant to everyday technology?
questions.answer: His paper explaining the photoelectric effect using light quanta — laying the foundation for solar cells, photo sensors, and quantum theory
choices: His paper explaining the photoelectric effect using light quanta — laying the foundation for solar cells, photo sensors, and quantum theory
His paper proving Earth has a magnetic field — leading directly to the global positioning system technology
His paper on circuit design — used immediately to manufacture telephones and the first electric lights
His paper on dental hygiene — funding his early career until his physics papers became more famous
questions.context: In 1905, Einstein published: special relativity (E=mc² as a corollary), Brownian motion (confirming atoms exist), the photoelectric effect (quantization of light), and his doctoral thesis. The photoelectric paper won him the 1921 Nobel — not relativity, which the Nobel committee considered too speculative at the time. The photoelectric effect explains how solar cells turn sunlight into electricity. Albert Einstein never received a Nobel for relativity; the 1921 award explicitly mentioned only the photoelectric work.

questions.question: Stephen Hawking spent most of his career in a wheelchair after ALS diagnosis at age 21 in 1963 (doctors gave him two years to live). His most famous theoretical contribution was about black holes. What did he discover?
questions.answer: Black holes emit radiation and slowly evaporate, what's now called Hawking radiation, due to quantum effects at the horizon
choices: Black holes emit radiation and slowly evaporate, what's now called Hawking radiation, due to quantum effects at the horizon
Black holes are actually flat disks, not three-dimensional, and the appearance of depth is an optical illusion
Black holes are connected to white holes elsewhere in the universe by direct tunnels through hyperspace
Black holes do not exist at all, and Hawking spent his career trying to disprove his own earlier claims
questions.context: Hawking's 1974 paper showed quantum field theory implies black holes radiate thermally. The radiation comes from pair creation near the event horizon: one particle escapes while its partner falls in, with the black hole losing mass equivalent to the escaped particle's energy. Solar-mass black holes evaporate over timescales much longer than the current age of the universe. Hawking radiation has never been directly detected but is widely accepted as theoretical fact. Hawking lived 55 years past his ALS diagnosis, dying in 2018 at 76.

questions.question: Albert Einstein's 1915 general relativity predicted gravity would bend starlight passing near the Sun. Who tested this in 1919, and what happened to Einstein's worldwide reputation as a result?
questions.answer: Arthur Eddington's eclipse expedition confirmed Einstein's prediction — making Einstein a global celebrity overnight
choices: Arthur Eddington's eclipse expedition confirmed Einstein's prediction — making Einstein a global celebrity overnight
Edwin Hubble tested it with his telescope — proving Einstein wrong and rejecting general relativity entirely
Marie Curie tested it with radioactivity measurements — confirming the basic theory by chemistry alone
It was never tested experimentally — Einstein's reputation grew through theoretical work only, not observation
questions.context: Eddington's May 29, 1919 expedition to Príncipe (and a parallel one to Sobral, Brazil) measured starlight bending during a total solar eclipse. The results matched Einstein's prediction (1.75 arcseconds) better than Newton's (half that). *The Times* of London ran 'Revolution in Science — New Theory of the Universe — Newtonian Ideas Overthrown.' Einstein became a global celebrity. Modern reanalysis of the original Eddington data has questioned whether 1919 alone could distinguish the theories confidently — but many later eclipses and radio measurements of quasars have confirmed Einstein's prediction with high precision.

questions.question: In November 2018 a Chinese researcher named He Jiankui announced he had used CRISPR to genetically edit twin baby girls (Lulu and Nana). How did the scientific community respond?
questions.answer: Widespread condemnation worldwide — He was later sentenced to three years in prison by Chinese courts
choices: Widespread condemnation worldwide — He was later sentenced to three years in prison by Chinese courts
Worldwide celebration — He was given a Nobel Prize and offered tenured positions at top universities
Indifference from researchers — most considered the case routine and unremarkable for genetic medicine
Acceptance but professional disapproval — He keeps his lab in Shenzhen and continues human gene editing today
questions.context: He Jiankui edited the CCR5 gene in human embryos at a Shenzhen lab, attempting to make the babies resistant to HIV. The Second International Summit on Human Genome Editing (Hong Kong, November 2018) condemned the experiment. He was tried, convicted, and sentenced to three years in prison in 2019. Doudna and others called the case a clear violation of consent, do-no-harm principles, and the international understanding that germline editing requires broad agreement before clinical use. He was released in 2022 and has remained active in genome-editing discussions.

questions.question: Therapeutic gene editing — CRISPR used to fix disease genes in patients who have already been born — is in a different ethical category from designer-baby germline editing. Why?
questions.answer: Therapeutic edits affect only the patient, with informed consent; germline edits change all future descendants without consent
choices: Therapeutic edits affect only the patient, with informed consent; germline edits change all future descendants without consent
Therapeutic edits are always banned worldwide; germline edits are encouraged universally for medical research
Therapeutic edits don't actually work; germline edits are the only effective form of CRISPR application
Therapeutic edits cause more side effects; germline edits are safer and considered the standard of care
questions.context: Casgevy (FDA-approved December 2023 for sickle cell) is a somatic-cell edit — affecting the patient's bone marrow only, not passed to offspring. Most clinical CRISPR trials target somatic cells. Germline editing changes egg, sperm, or embryo DNA — meaning every cell of the resulting person carries the edit AND it passes to children. The mainstream scientific community has not consensually approved germline editing for clinical use; He Jiankui's 2018 experiment broke that taboo. The therapeutic-germline ethical distinction is fundamental in modern bioethics.

questions.question: Gain-of-function research deliberately makes pathogens more dangerous (more transmissible or virulent) to study their potential. What's the policy debate about this kind of work?
questions.answer: Critics argue the lab-accident risk outweighs potential pandemic-preparedness benefits; the debate intensified post-COVID
choices: Critics argue the lab-accident risk outweighs potential pandemic-preparedness benefits; the debate intensified post-COVID
There is no debate, gain-of-function research has been universally banned worldwide since 2002
Gain-of-function research is required for all vaccine development, and no virus can be studied without it
Critics are universally dismissed by the scientific community, there is no respectable opposition to gain-of-function work
questions.context: The 2014-2017 US 'pause' on gain-of-function research applied to certain pathogens including influenza, SARS, and MERS. The pause lifted in 2017 under the new HHS framework requiring P3CO review (Potential Pandemic Pathogen Care and Oversight). Critics including Marc Lipsitch (Harvard), Richard Ebright (Rutgers), and others have argued the framework was applied with insufficient rigor. The COVID-19 origins controversy increased attention to this debate. As of 2025, Bhattacharya's NIH has paused new gain-of-function funding pending policy review.

questions.question: Twitter Files releases starting in late 2022 documented federal agency contacts with social media platforms during 2020-2022. What kind of scientific speech was suppressed under these contacts?
questions.answer: Discussion of lab leak, COVID treatments — vaccine side effects, and the Great Barrington Declaration were all flagged
choices: Discussion of lab leak, COVID treatments — vaccine side effects, and the Great Barrington Declaration were all flagged
Only flat-earth, anti-evolution, and chemtrails content was flagged — never any credentialed scientific work
No scientific content was ever flagged — only purely political speech with no medical implications at all
Discussion of dark matter — the Big Bang, and string theory were flagged as politically destabilizing topics
questions.context: The Twitter Files (Matt Taibbi, Bari Weiss, Michael Shellenberger, and others starting in November 2022) showed FBI, CDC, and other federal agencies routinely flagging accounts for suppression. Topics included natural-immunity discussions, vaccine adverse-event reports, lab-leak speculation, school-closure critiques, and Great Barrington Declaration content. Many flagged accounts belonged to credentialed scientists (Bhattacharya, Kulldorff, Vinay Prasad, Marty Makary). The Supreme Court's *Murthy v. Missouri* (2024) ruled on standing rather than reaching the merits of the First Amendment claim itself.

questions.question: The Murthy v. Missouri case in 2024 reached the US Supreme Court on the question of federal-government coordination with social-media platforms to suppress speech. What did the court ultimately rule?
questions.answer: The court ruled 6-3 that plaintiffs lacked standing, not reaching the underlying First Amendment question on the merits
choices: The court ruled 6-3 that plaintiffs lacked standing, not reaching the underlying First Amendment question on the merits
The court ruled unanimously that government-platform coordination is fully constitutional in every circumstance
The court ruled unanimously that any government-platform contact violates the First Amendment automatically
The court refused to hear the case at all, and the lower court ruling stood without modification or appeal
questions.context: *Murthy v. Missouri* (originally *Missouri v. Biden*) was filed by Missouri and Louisiana state attorneys general plus individual plaintiffs including Bhattacharya and Kulldorff. The 5th Circuit had ruled against the government. The Supreme Court (June 2024, Barrett writing for the majority) ruled 6-3 that plaintiffs lacked Article III standing — not addressing whether the government's conduct actually violated the First Amendment. Justice Alito dissented (joined by Thomas and Gorsuch), calling the case 'one of the most important free speech cases to reach this Court in years.' The merits remain open for future litigation.

questions.question: The Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) collects reports of suspected vaccine reactions in the US. What's the documented under-reporting problem with VAERS?
questions.answer: A 2010 Harvard Pilgrim study estimated less than 1% of actual vaccine adverse events are ever reported to VAERS
choices: A 2010 Harvard Pilgrim study estimated less than 1% of actual vaccine adverse events are ever reported to VAERS
VAERS captures essentially 100% of adverse events because of mandatory reporting requirements
VAERS overreports events by a factor of ten because the public uses it for unrelated medical complaints
VAERS does not exist, the US has never operated a vaccine adverse-event surveillance system
questions.context: VAERS is a passive surveillance system jointly run by CDC and FDA, open to reports from anyone. The 2010 Harvard Pilgrim Health Care study (a CMS-funded project led by Ross Lazarus) estimated 'fewer than 1% of vaccine adverse events are reported.' The CMS contract was not renewed; the planned electronic-tracking system was not built out. VAERS is widely cited in vaccine-safety discussions; critics including Kulldorff have called for improving its capture rate and integrating with electronic health records.

questions.question: Lysenkoism in the Soviet Union (1930s-1960s) is a famous case of politics destroying real science. What did Trofim Lysenko reject, and what was the human cost?
questions.answer: He rejected Mendelian genetics as 'bourgeois science' — and his ideas contributed to Soviet famines that killed millions
